academic-01__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
Urchin grazing, not temperature, is what controls kelp recovery in these fjords, and that finding should open the discussion.

## The shape that clicked
```
Old: context -> methods -> culling result -> variance -> crab -> future work
New:
  [Finding: urchins 61% vs temperature 4% of recovery variance]
        |
  [Culling test: 11% -> 58% cover; unculled sites flat]
        |
  [Context: drivers debated (Haugen; Lie & Strand)]
        |
  [Implication: target grazing; temperature range was not too narrow to detect an effect]
        |
  [Caveat: crab/access confound, stated and scoped]
        |
  [Bridge: Tasmania and California test whether this generalises]
```
The draft asks the reader to wait through context before the result. The result is the point, so it goes first. Temperature's 4% only means something once the reader knows sites varied by 2.1°C, so that detail moves up next to it.

## What moved
- Variance comparison (61% vs 4%): from the penultimate paragraph of results to the opening line, because it is the punchline.
- Culling result: from the middle of the paragraph to the second sentence, as the evidence for that claim.
- Temperature range (2.1°C): from the methods to the implication, because it defends the temperature null.
- Drivers and citations (Haugen 2009; Lie & Strand 2015): from the opening to the context paragraph, where they set up the debate the result resolves.
- Crab caveat (Moen et al. 2020): kept, placed after the main claim so it qualifies it.

**Cut:** "Understanding the relative contribution... remains an important goal" and "These results add to a growing body of work..." Both are generic and carry no citation or claim.

**Missing:**
- The effect size and uncertainty for the culled-site increase, such as a p-value or CI, which would be [placeholder].
- Whether the 61% and 4% come from the same model. I have assumed they do.
- Your Tasmania/California bridge sentence. The rebuild ends with a placeholder for it.
- Your own position on the management implication. My rebuild says grazing should be the priority; if you don't want to claim that yet, soften it.

Your co-supervisor's likely objection is that culled sites differed from unculled sites in more ways than urchin density, including crab-fisher access. The rebuilt caveat is designed to meet that objection before she raises it.

## Rebuilt

Urchin density, rather than sea temperature, was the strongest predictor of kelp recovery across the 24 sites we monitored in three fjords between 2018 and 2022. Where urchins were removed under the municipal culling programme, kelp canopy cover rose from a mean of 11% to 58% within three years. Unculled sites showed no significant change (9% to 12%), regardless of their temperature regime. In our mixed model, urchin density explained 61% of the variance in canopy recovery, compared with 4% for temperature, even though summer mean temperature varied across sites by up to 2.1°C.

Kelp declines along the northern Norwegian coast have been attributed to a combination of drivers, including sea urchin overgrazing, rising sea temperatures and changes in predator populations (Haugen 2009; Lie & Strand 2015). Our results suggest that, in these fjords, grazing pressure is the factor that moves canopy cover, and that restoration effort is best directed there. Crab presence was positively associated with recovery, but culled sites were also more accessible to crab fishers (Moen et al. 2020), so with these data we cannot separate that association from the effect of culling. [Bridge sentence to the Tasmania and California comparison.] Future work should examine the interaction between temperature and grazing pressure over longer timescales.

academic-01__base.text:
Your co-supervisor's margin note probably means the paragraph order hides your main result. The draft starts with the general problem, reports data, and only reaches the finding in the third paragraph. It ends by saying "multiple factors should be considered," which reads as a hedge. Your data make a stronger claim than that: urchin density explains far more of the recovery than temperature does. The restructured opening leads with that claim:

> Kelp forests along the northern Norwegian coast have declined substantially since the 1970s. Sea urchin overgrazing, rising temperatures and shifts in predator populations have all been proposed as causes (Haugen 2009; Lie & Strand 2015), but their relative importance remains unresolved, and it matters for management because each driver points to a different intervention.
>
> Our central result is that grazing pressure, not temperature, best predicted kelp recovery. At nine sites where urchins were removed under the municipal culling programme, mean canopy cover rose from 11% to 58% within three years. Fifteen unculled sites showed no significant change (9% to 12%), and this pattern held across a summer temperature range of up to 2.1°C. In our mixed model, temperature explained 4% of the variance in canopy recovery, compared with 61% for urchin density.
>
> Crab presence was also positively associated with recovery. However, culled sites were more accessible to crab fishers, so this association may partly reflect fishing access rather than a direct ecological effect (Moen et al. 2020).
>
> Taken together, these results identify urchin density as the most immediate lever for kelp restoration in these fjords, with temperature a weaker modifier within the range we sampled. The next section tests whether this pattern holds elsewhere by comparing our findings with studies from Tasmania and California. Limitations, including the non-random assignment of culling, are discussed afterwards.

Things to check before you send it back, since she may push on these:

- **Causal language.** Culling wasn't randomly assigned, so "grazing pressure best predicted recovery" is safer than "drove." The limitations section needs to address how culled and unculled sites were chosen and whether they differed at baseline (your starting cover was 11% vs 9%, which is close, but say so).
- **The crab confound.** You flagged fishing access, but you could check directly whether crab abundance differs between culled and unculled sites. If it does, the crab result needs more than a caveat.
- **The variance figures.** Make sure "4%" and "61%" are described correctly for your model (marginal or conditional R², or partial variance) and that the model specification is in the methods.
- **The "future work" sentence.** I moved the temperature × grazing interaction out of the opening. It fits better at the end of the discussion or in the limitations.

If she meant something different by "punchline," such as a specific implication for the municipal culling programme, let me know and I can rework it around that.

academic-02__skill_v1_1.text:
Summarising means one paragraph per source, in order. Synthesising means one paragraph per *idea*, with sources cited as evidence for or against it. Your reader wants to know what is known about why the policy isn't implemented. Adebayo is one piece of evidence for one part of that answer.

**A test for each paragraph:** ask "what does this tell me about my research question?" If the answer is "Adebayo studied X," it's a summary. If the answer is "the policy's rationale has evidence behind it, so non-implementation is probably not about efficacy," it's synthesis.

## A method for your 30+ sources

**1. Build an extraction table before writing.** One row per source, with columns for: author and year; state and school type (public or private, which level); design and sample; main finding; what it says about implementation or barriers; and whether it bears on Lagos private schools (yes, partly, or no). Your paragraph already gives you most of this.

**2. Group by mechanism, not by author or state.** Your question is "why," so the groups should be causes. From your chunk, plausible groups are:
- **Demand:** what parents and schools want (Ogunleye; Salami; Okonkwo and Eze on parental pressure)
- **Teacher supply:** who is able to teach in Yoruba (Adeyemi)
- **Materials:** whether books exist (Bello)
- **Drift in practice:** the policy is nominally met but diluted (Fashola's classes switching to English)
- **Evidence of benefit:** Adebayo and Ibrahim. This group is different. It is the background that makes non-implementation puzzling.

These groups are the parts of your argument, not the topics of your sources.

**3. Write one claim per group as a topic sentence.** A claim is something a reader could disagree with. "Parental demand for English is the most-reported barrier" is a claim. "Ogunleye interviewed 40 parents" is not.

**4. Under each claim, set out the evidence for, the evidence against or complicating it, and your judgement.** Cite each source where it supports that specific claim, and say which side is stronger and why.

**5. Map disagreements explicitly.** Adebayo (gains) and Fashola (no difference) conflict. Don't just list both. Ask what differs. Fashola's "Yoruba-medium" classes were mostly English for half the lesson time, so the conflict may be about what was actually delivered. That is a finding, and it points straight at your question. Similarly, Okonkwo and Eze (Anambra) and Ibrahim (Kano, Hausa) are not Yoruba or Lagos studies, so say how far the findings generalise.

**6. Look for the gap once the groups are built.** In your chunk, almost nothing concerns Lagos private schools specifically, and the decision to implement sits with private proprietors and principals, who are largely absent from the literature. Check whether that holds across your 30 sources. If it does, that absence is probably your contribution.

## What a synthesised paragraph might look like

Using only the findings you gave:

> The evidence that mother-tongue instruction helps is mixed but present. Adebayo (2014) found numeracy gains for Yoruba-taught pupils in Oyo State, and Ibrahim (2019) reported early literacy gains in Hausa-medium classes in Kano. Fashola (2018) found no difference in Lagos, but her data also show that most "Yoruba-medium" classes used English for over half of lesson time. The disagreement may therefore be less about the method than about whether the method was delivered at all.

That paragraph makes a claim, uses sources as evidence, and says what the disagreement means. The rest of the chapter can then ask why delivery fails, which is where the demand-side and teacher-supply groups come in.

If you paste the rest of your sources, or start the extraction table, I can help you sort them into groups and find the gap.

academic-02__base.text:
Nobody teaches this well, and "synthesise, don't summarise" is vague advice. Here's what it means in practice.

## Summary vs. synthesis

- **Summary** is organised by source: *Study A did X, Study B did Y, Study C found Z.* The reader learns about the studies but has to do the thinking.
- **Synthesis** is organised by claim: *Evidence suggests X, though Y complicates it.* Each study is evidence for a point you're making.

A quick test: if you can swap the author names around and the paragraph still reads fine, you've written a summary. Your topic sentences should be claims, not sources.

## Organise by argument, not by author, state, or date

Grouping by state or topic can work, but neither is an argument. Organise by the logic of your research question. Your question is *why* the policy isn't implemented in Lagos private schools, which suggests a structure like this:

1. **Does the policy matter?** Evidence that mother-tongue instruction helps learning (Adebayo, Ibrahim). Establishes stakes.
2. **Is it being delivered?** Evidence of what actually happens in classrooms and what supports exist (Fashola, Bello, Adeyemi).
3. **Why might it not be delivered?** Demand-side pressures: parents, markets, private school branding (Ogunleye, Salami, Okonkwo & Eze).
4. **Where's the gap?** What nobody has studied yet, which is your justification.

Each section is a sub-argument. Your 30 extra sources slot into these themes.

## A method for your 30+ sources

1. **Build an extraction matrix** (a spreadsheet). One row per source. Columns: author/year, location, public or private, sample, method, main finding, and a column called "what this says about implementation." That last column is the one that turns summary into synthesis.
2. **Sort and cluster.** Sort by theme, and by school type and location. Patterns will show up quickly.
3. **Look for disagreements.** This is the most valuable step. Adebayo finds gains and Fashola finds none. Those conflicts are where your argument lives. Ask *why* they differ: different location, different school type, or, as Fashola's finding suggests, the treatment wasn't actually delivered as designed.
4. **Write one question per theme:** "What do these studies collectively show?" Your answer is your topic sentence.
5. **Note what's missing.** If nothing studies Lagos private schools specifically, say so. That's your gap, and it justifies your research.

## Applied to your chunk

Here's a rough paragraph to show the move. Notice that the claim comes first and the sources serve it:

> Evidence that mother-tongue instruction supports early learning is fairly consistent, but its benefits may depend on whether it is delivered as designed. Adebayo (2014) reports numeracy gains for pupils taught in Yoruba through P3, yet Fashola (2018) finds no difference when replicating the design in Lagos, and notes that "Yoruba-medium" classes switched to English for over half of lesson time. These studies do not test implementation directly, but read together they suggest the policy's effects may be diluted before they can be measured. This raises the question of what constrains delivery, which the following studies address from the supply side: materials were absent from 78% of sampled schools (Bello 2017), and none of five colleges of education offered a methods course in an indigenous language (Adeyemi 2021).

Things to notice:
- The first sentence is the claim. The sources come after it.
- Fashola's finding is used to *complicate* Adebayo, not just list alongside it.
- The hedging ("may," "suggest," "do not test directly") is deliberate. It keeps you honest about what the studies can and can't show.
- The last sentence links to the next theme, so the paragraphs form an argument rather than a list.

One caution: Okonkwo & Eze (Anambra) and Ibrahim (Kano, Hausa) are outside your Yoruba/Lagos focus. You can use them as contrast or context, but say explicitly why they're relevant, or your reader will wonder.

If you paste in a few more summaries, or your current section headings, I can help you cluster them into themes.

talk-05__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

Homework counts for 20% of the grade and students from low-income families complete it at much lower rates, so homework load is a fairness problem as well as a stress problem. Lincoln's pilot suggests a 30-minute cap did not cost test performance.

## The shape that clicked

```
Gradebook gap: 88% vs 61% completion, homework = 20% of grade
        │
        ▼
Question: does a cap cost learning?  ── Lincoln: scores flat, D/F 19% → 12%
        │
        ▼
What a cap frees: 3–4 hrs/week of ELA grading
        │
        ▼
Student stress: the voice that confirms the problem, not the proof
```

Your colleague's point: the stress survey is the hook and the closing, so the whole case leans on it. It is 51 optional responses from two class periods, which is about 37 students saying "stressed." A math teacher can dismiss that in one sentence, and then the case looks soft even though the gradebook data is much stronger. The best evidence is in the middle of your notes.

## What moved

- **Gradebook gap**: from the middle to the opening, because it is your district's own data and nobody can call it self-selected.
- **Lincoln pilot**: from the middle to second place, because it answers the question the room will ask: "what happens if we cap it?"
- **Teacher time**: from the middle to a practical payoff section, because it is the concrete benefit to the people in the room.
- **Stress survey**: from the opening and closing to one supporting paragraph, framed as a symptom.
- **Parent emails**: cut from the main argument. Mention them only if asked.
- **Research review**: from the middle to one sentence. "Research is mixed for middle school" is a reason to pilot, not a reason to cap.
- **Cut**: "Our kids are telling us something" as the closing line. Replace it with a call to action.
- **Missing**: (a) whether the completion gap comes from time, access to materials, or grading policy, since a cap only helps if volume is the cause; (b) whether Lincoln's team and comparison group were similar, and what else changed that year; (c) what teachers would actually assign under a cap.

## Rebuilt

**Opening (full text):**
"In our three middle schools, homework is 20% of most grades. Students not on free or reduced lunch complete it 88% of the time; students who are complete it 61% of the time. That gap goes straight onto report cards. I'm proposing a 30-minute nightly cap on total homework across subjects, and I want to show you why I think it's a fairness decision and not only a workload one."

**Outline:**

1. **The gap (gradebook data).** Show the completion numbers and the report-card effect. Ask: what is homework measuring?
2. **Does a cap cost learning? (Lincoln).** Lincoln's 7th grade team capped homework quietly last year. ELA moved +1 and math -1 on state tests, and D/F rates fell from 19% to 12%. State plainly: this was one team, not a controlled study, and we don't know what else changed. The claim is "no measurable loss," not "the cap caused the drop in D/Fs."
3. **What a cap frees (teacher time).** Grading homework takes our ELA teachers roughly 3–4 hours a week (my estimate; [insert a more precise figure if you can get one]). Show what that time could go to instead.
4. **What students say (survey).** Be exact: 51 optional responses from two sections, 72% reported feeling stressed or very stressed. Present it as a sign that the load is felt, and say you would want a broader survey before the district decides.
5. **What the cap does not do.** Name this yourself before anyone else does. It doesn't guarantee completion rates rise, and it doesn't settle what the right amount of homework is.
6. **The ask.** A pilot or a vote, with a named review date and [the metrics you'll track].

**Preparing for math:** Expect them to open with the -1 in math. Name it first, in one line: "Math moved -1 at Lincoln, which is within the noise, but I'd rather you hear it from me." The cap is a total budget across subjects, not a ban, so math keeps the ability to choose how its share is spent. Ask them to propose what their 30 minutes should look like rather than arguing against the number in the abstract. Teachers who are pro-homework usually respond better to being asked to design within the constraint than to being told the constraint is settled.

academic-03__base.text:
You can keep both, but not as two parallel findings. Right now the intro is a literature review for two papers. The fix is to find the single question that both results answer.

**My view: lead with the informal wage result, and treat disemployment as the formal-sector side of the same mechanism.**

The reasoning:

- Your results form one story. The floor raises the reference wage. Formal employers cut low-wage positions (-1.8%). Some of those workers move into informality (+3.1%). The informal wage rises too (+4.2%), because the floor now anchors informal pay. Total employment is unchanged. The disemployment number is a shift in *where* employment happens, not a loss of jobs.
- The "masked disemployment" line in your paragraph 1 is already close to this. Your co-author is right that referees care about the employment literature, but the paper's distinctive claim is about where the floor's incidence lands when most low-wage workers are outside its legal reach.
- The disemployment estimate is small and standard, as you say. Leading with it makes the paper look like a standard minimum-wage paper with a footnote. Leading with the spillover makes the formal decline the cost side of a result the literature doesn't already have.

So the organizing question should be something like: *when a minimum wage binds in a formal sector that is only a fraction of the labour market, where does the adjustment fall?* Disemployment is one answer (formal, small, offset by informal). Informal wage spillover is the other.

**Sketch of the first two paragraphs:**

> In economies where most low-wage work is informal, a minimum wage applies to only part of the labour market, and the adjustment may not appear where standard models look for it. Employment effects measured in formal records can show job losses that are offset by informal work, while the legal floor may matter for workers it does not cover. This paper asks where the incidence of a regional wage floor falls in Brazil's Northeast, where formal employment is a minority of low-wage work.

> We study a 2017 wage floor set 14% above the national minimum in three northeastern states. Using a synthetic control design with RAIS and PNAD data, we find that formal employment among workers earning below 1.5 times the floor fell by 1.8%, while informal employment in the same occupations rose by 3.1% and total employment was essentially unchanged. Informal earnings in affected occupations rose by 4.2%, despite no legal obligation to pay the floor. The formal decline is thus a reallocation across sectors, and the floor operates as a reference point for informal pay, consistent with a lighthouse effect (Souza 2011; Neri et al. 2015).

Then paragraph 3 can say the paper contributes to the lighthouse literature by showing it with a causal design and by linking it to formal-sector adjustment, and to the employment literature by showing that the employment margin is a sectoral shift rather than a net loss.

**Before you send this to referees, I'd resolve three things, because they'll come up:**

1. **Composition.** The 4.2% informal earnings rise could come from workers with higher unobserved productivity moving into informal jobs, not from pay rising for the same workers. Show the result with worker-level controls, or with a fixed-composition panel, or at least discuss the direction of the bias. This is the most likely referee objection to the headline result.
2. **Inference with three treated units.** Synthetic control with three treated states needs placebo-in-space and placebo-in-time tests, and you should report how sensitive the 1.8% and 4.2% estimates are to the donor pool. A 1.8% effect significant at 5% is fragile under that scrutiny.
3. **Conclusion.** It should return to the single question from the intro: where the incidence landed, and what that implies for the floor's effectiveness in a mostly informal labour market. If the conclusion discusses the two results separately, it will reproduce the stapled structure.

Your co-author's instinct about referees is reasonable. The way to satisfy it is to show that the employment result is one side of the spillover mechanism, not a separate finding. That keeps the connection to the employment literature while making the informal wage result the paper's main contribution.

strategy-07__base.text:
Your draft is trying to avoid a choice that your own numbers have already made. "Equal energy" is impossible with 14 content people and one big restructuring a year, so the team will read the note as "do everything" and keep working on whatever they were already doing. The note should say which bet wins, what gets deferred, and why.

Some of your unlisted numbers also change the story:

- **31% of B2C paid users come from a school that uses Padhai.** A large share of the consumer business is a school channel. Framing B2C as an independent consumer company at heart is probably inaccurate.
- **B2C economics are weakening.** CAC more than doubled in 18 months (₹410 to ₹780), and 9% monthly churn is high. A ₹199 tier and vernacular content are bets on acquiring more users at a worse price.
- **The content constraint forces a choice.** Teachers want state-board alignment, which is the school product. Vernacular expansion is mainly a B2C growth bet. You can't do both, so the note has to rank them.

**On the founders:** I'd avoid "pick schools" as the headline. Instead, lead with what the consumer business did (it built parent trust and a brand, and it is now the top of the school funnel) and then show that the economics have moved. Put the churn and CAC numbers in the note itself. If the founders discover them later, the note loses credibility. Talk to the founders 1:1 before the offsite so the discussion there is about trade-offs rather than the premise.

**Draft:**

**Padhai: Where we're going in 2025**

Our consumer product earned us something valuable: 1.2M registered learners, 86k paying families, and parents who trust Padhai with their children's maths. That trust is now our most important asset, and it is what schools buy into.

The data says schools are where we grow. Our 140 partner schools generate ₹3.4 crore ARR at 81% gross margin, against 52% for direct B2C. School contracts are annual, and once a chain signs, acquisition cost is close to zero. Nearly a third of our paying B2C families came through a school, so the school channel also feeds consumer retention.

Direct B2C is getting more expensive. CAC has risen from ₹410 to ₹780 in 18 months, and monthly paid churn is ~9%. We will not scale paid acquisition until retention improves.

**Decision for 2025:** Our 14-person content team has capacity for one major restructuring. We will use it for state-board alignment and a teacher dashboard, because that is what schools are asking for and what drives our growth. Vernacular content (Kannada, Tamil, Hindi) and the ₹199 tier are deferred to H2 and will be reconsidered once school alignment ships and B2C retention is above [target].

**What we will measure:** school ARR and renewals, school-to-B2C conversion, B2C monthly churn, and CAC payback.

**Before you circulate:**
- Confirm the 31% figure and how "acquired through school" is defined, since it will be the note's central fact.
- Add total company ARR so schools' share is visible. You have school ARR but not the B2C total.
- Set the retention target that unlocks vernacular and the ₹199 tier. Without a number, "deferred" becomes "cancelled" quietly, or the founders will read it as a temporary pause.
- Decide what happens to the B2C team. If the consumer story matters to the founders, give them a real job: protecting retention and the brand that feeds schools.

life-decision-10__skill_v1_1.text:
**The spine:** You're considering a move that would change Callum's week, and you want to hear Fiona's view before you answer by the 28th.

The talking points are arranged as "decision made, benefits, please agree." That's why the conversation went sideways last time: the biggest issue, changing the 50/50, is apologised for at the end, and Callum's happiness is listed as a reason to stay rather than as the thing that matters most. The shape that should hold is "undecided, here's what it would mean for Callum, here's what I don't know yet, I want your view."

## What moved

- **Point 6 (part-remote, unconfirmed):** moved to the top, and it should be confirmed with HR before Sunday. Everything else depends on it.
- **Points 1 and 9:** combined. Lead with the salary net of London rent, not the gross figure.
- **Point 7 (changing the 50/50):** moved up front and stated plainly, not apologised for at the end.
- **Point 10 (Callum's football):** moved to the centre. It's the strongest point you have and the one she'll weigh most.
- **Point 5 (£400/month):** cut from this conversation. If it comes up, it reads as paying for agreement. Let her raise money if she wants to.
- **Points 3 and 4:** reframed as options to discuss, not plans to announce.
- **Point 2 and "I just need to get Fiona on board":** cut. If you go in needing her yes, you'll hear her concerns as obstacles.

## Rebuilt: rough script

*"Thanks for meeting. I want to talk about the job offer in London. I haven't accepted, and I don't want to until we've talked properly, because it would change Callum's weeks and that's yours and mine to work out.*

*Here's what I know. It's Head of Operations UK, salary £84k against £58k now. HR have said the role could probably be done two or three days a week in London and the rest remote, but they haven't confirmed that. I'm checking that before I decide anything.*

*Here's what I don't know. London rent for somewhere Callum could stay would take a big chunk of the raise. I don't know yet whether it works. [Insert your rent figures if you have them.]*

*I know it would mean changing the 50/50. I'm not going to pretend it doesn't. I'd want to be in Callum's life a lot, with school holidays and regular weekends, but I know that's not the same as him being with me every other week, and I'm not going to sell it as if it were.*

*Callum's just settled into his new football club and he seems really happy. I don't want to take that away from him without being sure.*

*So I want to hear what you think. What worries you most? What would have to be true for you to be okay with it, if anything? And if you'd rather I didn't go, I need to hear that too. I'll give you my answer by the 28th, and I'd rather get it right than rush it."*

## Before Sunday

- **Confirm the remote arrangement in writing with HR.** Don't present it as settled until it is.
- **Check what your current arrangement is.** If it's a court order or a formal agreement, a change of residence or a big change to the 50/50 may need Fiona's written consent or a court variation. A short call with a Scottish family solicitor before you agree anything verbally would protect both you and Callum.
- **Decide your answer if she says no.** Work out now whether you'd turn the job down, negotiate something else, or ask for a remote-only role. Going in without that will make the conversation feel like a test.
- **Think about Callum's view.** At nine he should be heard, but not asked to choose or carry the decision. How and when to involve him is worth talking through with Fiona.

life-decision-06__base.text:
The table isn't working because you're mixing four different questions, and half the items answer different ones.

**1. Do you want to farm?** This is the one that feels like it should be the whole decision, but it's only one piece. Your "I genuinely miss it" is real information, but it's about the work and the place. It doesn't tell you whether the economics or your family can carry it.

**2. Can the operation support your family?** Look at the numbers:
- Jake's cash rent offer is about $290 × 640 acres ≈ **$186k/year** to your dad, with no labor and no risk.
- Your five-year average farm net income is about **$94k/year**, and it swings from -$15k to $210k.

Unless dad's labor is already baked into that $94k, renting the ground out may pay the family more than farming it. That matters because it means your return on coming back is mostly about the things rent doesn't give you: the work, the place, the family continuity. Those can be worth a lot, but they should be weighed deliberately, not assumed. You'd also be taking on a combine replacement and other capital costs. Get a real P&L from dad and ask whether it's before or after his own wages.

**3. Can your family handle the move?** This is Priya, the kids, the house, insurance, and school. Your list is a mess mostly because of this one. "Schools are fine" and "Denver schools are better" can both be true. Priya's "open but nervous" is the most important sentence on the list, and right now it's the one you're least able to act on. Have a specific conversation with her: what would she need to feel okay, what would a trial period look like, what happens if it doesn't work.

**4. What do you owe dad, and what do you want to give him?** This is where the guilt lives. Guilt is a good reason to talk to your dad. It's a bad reason to decide. Also notice that dad's offer, a contract sale over a few years, is a deal you could accept or counter, not a verdict on whether you're family.

**What to say at Thanksgiving:** You don't have to give a yes or no. Something like: "I want to do this seriously. Here's what I need to figure out before I can say yes, and here's a timeline." Then propose a real option. For example:
- A one-to-two-year trial where you work the farm while you keep Denver as a fallback
- A lease-to-own structure rather than an immediate contract sale
- Renting to Jake now with an option for you to take over later

Also ask him what he actually wants. He may care most that the land stays in the family, or that he's not alone, or that someone he trusts is running it. Those point to different answers, and some don't require you to move at all.

**Before Thanksgiving, get:**
- The real operating P&L, including what dad's labor is worth
- The combine and equipment replacement plan and cost
- Jake's rental terms written out, so you know your fallback
- Your health insurance cost on the open market, plus any farm-business coverage
- A real conversation with Priya about her conditions, not her general mood

If you do that, the question changes from "do I want to be the guy who comes back to the farm?" to "under what terms would this work for my family, and am I willing to take that on?" That's a question you can actually answer, and it's the one you can take to dad.

life-decision-02__base.text:
Here's a restructured version that puts the news in the first two paragraphs, so they know what the email is about right away:

---

Dear Amma and Appa,

I hope you are both well, and that Appa's knee is improving with the physiotherapy.

I have some big news, and I wanted to tell you myself. I have accepted a position as a senior backend engineer with Nordlicht Mobility in Berlin, and I start on 3rd March.

I know this is far from Coimbatore, and I know how happy you were when I joined Corvane and could be home for Pongal and Deepa's wedding. I'm sorry I didn't talk to you before accepting. The deadline was very short, and I didn't want to worry you about something that might not happen.

The decision came from a few things. Over the past year my growth here has slowed. My manager has changed twice, and the project I was hired for was shut down. I have also been learning German on weekends, which I didn't mention because I wasn't sure it would lead anywhere. This feels like the right next step for my career.

Going abroad doesn't change my responsibility to you both. I will keep sending money every month, and I expect to send more now that the salary is higher. I will come home at least once a year, and maybe twice. If anything happens with your health, I will fly back immediately.

I would really like to talk this through with you properly. Could I call you this Sunday? I want to hear what you think, and answer any questions you have.

With love,
Karthik

---

A few notes:

- **Call them too.** For a traditional family, big news often lands better when they hear it from you directly, not only in writing. You could send the email, then call the same day or the next. Or call first and let the email follow as a written record they can read again.
- **Consider a heads-up to Deepa** or another relative they trust, so they aren't blindsided if they talk to people in Coimbatore before they hear from you.
- **Be ready for the first reaction to be emotional or worried**, even if they're proud. Your reassurance about money and visits will matter most to them, so you may need to repeat it on the call.

life-decision-01__base.text:
You've been going round in circles because the list doesn't weigh things. Some items are small and some are large, and the lists treat them as equal.

**What I think your list is telling you**

- **The back is the heaviest item, and it's on the wrong side.** Your physio said that if you keep doing manual handling on 12.5-hour shifts, you'll probably need surgery within a couple of years. You've already had six weeks off this year. That isn't a lifestyle preference. It's a warning about your body and your career. Halvern's job removes the manual handling, though it may add prolonged sitting in the car, which can also aggravate discs. Ask your physio about that specifically.
- **The pension is less absolute than your mum thinks.** Your NHS pension benefits built up so far are preserved if you leave, and you can rejoin the NHS later. What you'd lose is future accrual and the employer contribution, which is generous. Get the real figures from NHS Pensions and compare them with whatever Halvern offers. Don't assume.
- **The money may be closer than it looks.** Your £38.7k probably excludes or understates unsocial hours payments, and Halvern's package includes a car, which is taxed as a benefit, and a bonus that may not be guaranteed. Work out actual take-home for both roles, including pension contributions.
- **Your "cons" are mostly unknowns, not reasons.** "Sales targets scare me" is real but specific. "Feels like selling out" is a feeling about identity. "What if I hate it" is a fear you can test.
- **The sick feeling is worth paying attention to, but it doesn't tell you which way to go.** It could mean you don't want to leave, or that you're scared of failing, or that you feel guilty about leaving people you love. Those lead to different decisions.

**What you're missing**

1. **What the job actually is day to day.** What are the targets, how are they measured, what's the base versus commission split, and what's the probation period? Ask for it in writing.
2. **Whether the back problem changes if you stay.** Could you move to a lower-handling role, get lifting aids, or reduce 12.5s? If the ward can't offer that, the back argument for leaving gets stronger.
3. **Whether you'd regret each choice in five years.** Imagine both are fine. Which one do you picture yourself at, and which one do you feel relief about?
4. **A test of your reasons.** If your best mate and your partner had no opinion, and your back were fine, which would you choose? Your answer tells you whether the sick feeling is about the job or about other people.

**Before Friday**

- Ask Halvern for the full written contract, the pension details, and the target structure. A reasonable employer won't object.
- Ask Halvern whether you can speak to someone currently in the role. Ask them how many people hit target and what the first year looks like.
- Ask your ward manager for a concrete timeline and criteria for band 7, not "possibly."
- Ask your physio what they'd recommend about your job, and whether you should get a referral now regardless of what you decide.
- If the deadline is firm, ask Halvern whether a short extension is possible. Many employers accept a few extra days for a decision like this.

I'd be cautious about deciding purely on the basis of "I love my team" versus "more money and less driving." Your team matters, and you can stay in touch with them outside work. Your back and your daughter are time-sensitive in a way the ward isn't. But I'd also take the sick feeling seriously. It may be telling you something about the job itself, or about your own fear of change.

If you tell me what the targets look like, what the physio actually said about your disc, and what your net pay difference is, I can help you run the numbers more concretely.

positioning-08__base.text:
**I'd back a sharpened version of Route A, built around the renewal cap rather than price at point of sale.** I'd call it something like "No nasty renewal surprises" with the 8% cap as the proof point.

**Why this, and not C or B**

- **Your survey points at renewal.** Premium jumps at renewal are the biggest frustration (61%). Price at purchase is last (14%). The 44% who switched or cancelled over a renewal increase show this is behaviour, not just complaint. Route A as written, "cover that doesn't cost the earth," is aimed at the 14%.
- **You already have the answer to the 61%, and nobody uses it.** An 8% annual cap on lifetime policies, regardless of age, speaks directly to the biggest pain point. Competitors can't claim it without changing their pricing, so it's harder to copy than a service claim.
- **Route C is weakening.** Only 19% cite slow claims, and two competitors now say "same day." A speed claim you can't win on headline is a weak headline. Keep the 48-hour stat as supporting evidence.
- **Route B is good credibility but doesn't answer the top frustration.** Your vet panel is a reason to believe, so it belongs in the support copy, not the lead.

**How I'd frame it for Friday**

Lead with the problem the market already told you about: "Most pet insurers raise your premium every year your pet gets older. Ours can't go up more than 8% a year, for as long as you hold the policy." Then:
- Vets on the panel as the reason the product is built this way (support line).
- 48-hour claims as the second proof point.
- Price stays in the background. You're mid-market, so don't sell on being cheapest.

**Check these before you commit to it**

1. **Exact wording of the cap.** Does 8% cover the whole premium or only the age-related element? Are there other triggers for increases (claims history, IPT or vet fee changes, general repricing)? If the cap has exceptions, the headline can't say "never more than 8%" without qualification.
2. **Lifetime-only and tier-switch conditions.** These must appear in the ads, not only on page 6. Under FCA rules (Consumer Duty and financial promotions), a headline claim that omits material conditions is a compliance risk and an ASA complaint waiting to happen.
3. **Finance's view of the cost.** Your underwriter agreed to the cap, so it's presumably priced in, but get finance to model its cost at scale. If finance is comfortable, the "fair price" story is strengthened rather than contradicted.
4. **The 44% figure.** Check the sample size for the over-8s subgroup and confirm the question wording before it goes on a slide.
5. **Survey base.** It's owners generally, not your customers. That's fine for market insight but not for claiming what your customers think.

**For the room**

- To the agency: C is a good fight, but it's a fight you're late to. The renewal problem is bigger and you own the answer.
- To finance: this is a fair-price story, specifically the one that matters to people, and it's already in your terms.
- To the founder: the vet panel is in the campaign, as the reason the product works this way.

The risk to flag is that the cap is a promise. If it's marketed loudly and the fine print causes complaints at renewal, you'll lose the trust you're trying to win. So the campaign has to be as precise as the T&Cs.

talk-10__base.text:
Your draft is organised as a investigation, with the answer at the end. Officials making a decision need the answer first. Your PI is right that slide 8 alone undersells the study, but the fix is not to make the voice result look bigger. The fix is to make the study's real contribution the centre of the talk: SMS as tested doesn't work, and you've found where the coverage gap actually comes from.

## Restructure: lead with the decision

**Slide 1: Bottom line.** Put the recommendation here, stated plainly:
- SMS reminders alone did not raise full immunisation. Don't scale them as they are.
- Voice reminders showed a promising signal in one district. It needs a proper test before any decision to scale.
- Most missed doses happen at the measles-rubella second dose, and the families involved are often migrating. Reminders aimed at that window and at that problem are the next thing to test.

Then say what you need from the officials: a decision on whether to fund a confirmatory trial and a migration-window pilot.

**Slide 2: The gap.** Keep your current problem slide, but make the title about where the gap sits, not only its size. For example: "Coverage is 70% against a 90% target, and the drop-off is concentrated at 16–24 months."

**Slide 3: What we tested.** Design only. Show the three arms, the sample size, and the timing. Say clearly that the voice arm was added partway through and runs in one district only. This is your credibility move: state the limitation before they find it.

**Slide 4: Primary result.** Title it with the finding: "SMS reminders did not change full immunisation coverage (70.2% vs 71.0%)." Show the confidence interval, not just the p-value. A narrow interval around zero is a useful result because it rules out a meaningful benefit. Make the null informative, not apologetic.

**Slide 5: Why reach failed.** Your three reasons (husbands' phones, shared phones, literacy) are good evidence that the intervention didn't reach the mother. If you have any data on whether messages were received or read, add it here, since it separates "the message never arrived" from "it arrived and didn't change behaviour."

**Slide 6: Where dropout happens.** This is your most useful slide and should be given the most time. Missed MR2 doses cluster in the 16–24 month window, and 60% of those families reported seasonal migration for brick kiln or construction work. Reminders to a phone number that may not reach the family during migration cannot solve this. Frame it as a finding about the problem, not as a failure of the intervention.

**Slide 7: Voice arm, labelled as exploratory.** Title it: "An exploratory signal in one district, not yet a finding." Show 79.5% vs 70.8% with its confidence interval, and note:
- It was not part of the original design and was added late.
- It compares arms within one district, so it can't be generalised yet.
- The no-schooling subgroup (+14 points) is a subgroup finding. Include it only with an interaction test, or leave it out of the main talk. Don't lead with it.

Say what would make this credible: a pre-registered confirmatory trial across both districts with voice as the primary comparison.

**Slide 8: Cost per outcome.** Costs alone mislead. SMS at ₹4 per child per year buys nothing if it has no effect. Voice at ₹19 is only worth it if the effect is real. A rough indicative figure: if the voice effect held at about 8.7 points, the cost is roughly ₹200–250 per additional fully immunised child per year. Label this as indicative and assumption-dependent, and show the confidence bounds if you can. Ask the officials which cost per additional child they would accept.

**Slide 9: Recommendations, tiered.**
1. **Stop:** scaling SMS-only reminders.
2. **Test:** a confirmatory voice-reminder trial across both districts, pre-registered, with coverage as the primary outcome.
3. **Pilot:** a migration-window intervention targeting MR2, such as portable immunisation cards, catch-up at destination sites, outreach through labour contractors or brick kilns, and verifying the phone number on the family's register.
4. **Low-cost now:** check and correct registered phone numbers and confirm who holds each phone, since 38% belonged to someone else.

**Slide 10: The ask.** One sentence on the decision you need, with a date.

## On your PI's concern

Officials stopping at slide 8 is only a problem if slide 8 is the wrong slide. If the first slide gives the bottom line and the last slide repeats it with the decision, a reader who stops early still gets the right message: don't scale SMS, look at migration, test voice properly. That is a better outcome than either a spun success or a bare null.

Twelve minutes is about 8 to 10 slides with discussion, so you may need to merge 3 and 5, and fold 8 into 9 if time is tight. Keep slide 6 and the decision slide regardless.

team-09__base.text:
The COO's comment points to a structural problem. Your paper is organised around the systems, so it reads as an evaluation of products. A management committee needs it organised around the decision, the cost of the status quo, and the options against that cost. Here's how I'd restructure it.

## Proposed structure

**1. The decision and recommendation (first half-page)**
- State the ask: "Approve consolidation of document management on a single platform (Option A), at a net incremental cost of SGD X per year, over 18 months."
- Give the reason in two or three sentences: fragmentation costs the firm an estimated SGD Y in non-billable search time and creates a demonstrated risk of using outdated precedents.
- Say what happens if the committee does nothing. This is the strongest framing you have.

**2. The problem: what fragmentation costs us**
- Lead with the time study and the Jakarta near-misses, since the risk is the non-financial case that matters most to partners.
- Present the time study with its method and limits: 36 associates, two weeks, one month. Show the Bangkok/Jakarta gap (6.1 vs 4.6 hours).
- Keep the cross-office finding (31% of searches fail entirely) separate from the general search time, because it measures a different thing.

**3. Options compared on decision criteria**
Compare the options on criteria the committee cares about, not on product features:
- Net annual cost (incremental to today)
- Time to realise benefit
- Precedent-risk exposure
- Disruption to fee earners
- Dependence on a single vendor

A table with A, B and C as columns and these criteria as rows works well. Options B and C need the same cost treatment as A, and I'd check whether the paper currently gives B a cost figure.

**4. Recommendation and rationale**
Explain why A beats B and C against the criteria above. Acknowledge what B does well. Keep the rationale short.

**5. Implementation, risks and safeguards**
Move the timeline, change management and mitigations here. This section is where you answer the DocuNest partners.

**Appendix:** the 14-criteria feature table, the full time-study methodology, and the cost workings.

## Points to fix before the committee sees it

**The cost framing is probably overstating the ask.** You describe the request as the extra spend, but the relevant figure is the net change. LexVault at SGD 465k replaces LexVault at SGD 310k plus DocuNest at SGD 95k (SGD 405k total). That's roughly SGD 60k net per year, before any SharePoint or M365 adjustments. If that's right, it's the most persuasive number in the paper, and it should appear in the first half-page. Check it carefully, though, because the committee will.

**The SGD 9–10M figure needs defending.** It's the number most likely to be challenged and to damage credibility if it doesn't hold. Check:
- The headcount base. SGD 9–10M at 4.6–6.1 hours a week and SGD 180/hour implies roughly 200+ associates. Confirm the population and whether the sample is representative.
- The cost basis. Non-billable time is an opportunity cost, not a cash saving. Say so, and show how much would be recoverable through redeployment to billable work.
- Whether the blended rate applies to Bangkok and Jakarta, where rates are likely lower.

Consider presenting a conservative case (for example, only the Bangkok/Jakarta uplift, or only recoverable hours) alongside the headline. A range you have stress-tested will be more credible than a single figure.

**Address the DocuNest partners directly, but in the right place.** Don't write a section defending LexVault against DocuNest. In the options analysis, show what B's federated search would cost and what it would fail to solve (the cross-office version problem). In the implementation section, set out what protects Jakarta's workflows and matter continuity during migration. Partners are more likely to support a plan that addresses their concerns than one that argues against their tool.

**Anticipate the COO's likely questions.** Before resubmitting, have answers ready for: what happens if we do nothing, what the exit or fallback is if migration goes wrong, and what the first 90 days look like.

If you share the cost tables or the time-study breakdown, I can help you build the summary table and check the arithmetic.

life-decision-08__base.text:
Your reasoning is clear and your cost base is reasonable, but the revenue case isn't yet solid enough to bet your household on. Your wife is pointing at the same weak spots I see, so her concern is probably more than general risk aversion.

## What holds up

- **The cost structure is modest and specific.** A four-person firm in Westlands is a sensible scale to start at.
- **You know the Tarvo work and the relationship.** Four years of contracts work is real expertise and goodwill.
- **You've thought about the draw.** Accepting a lower income is the right instinct.

## Where the case is weak

**1. Concentration on one unsigned client.** Tarvo is 59% of projected revenue, and "we'd definitely consider moving with you" is not a mandate. GCs say this often, and moves depend on procurement rules, panel reviews, budget cycles, and whether the GC's position survives a reorganisation. If Tarvo doesn't move, your revenue drops to about 6.7M a year, or roughly 560k a month, against fixed costs of 955k. That's a gap of about 400k a month, or 4.8M a year.

**2. Kilima is also not a mandate.** A friendly MD from law school is a warm lead, not a signed engagement. Together, Tarvo and Kilima are 12.8M, which is barely above your 11.5M annual cost base. Almost nothing is left to absorb delays, write-offs, or tax.

**3. The non-solicitation clause is a real risk.** Your friend's view that these are "hard to enforce" is not legal advice. Kenyan courts assess restraints for reasonableness, and an injunction or damages claim could land exactly when you're trying to onboard your biggest client. Beyond the legal exposure, a dispute with your current firm over its clients can follow you in a small market. Before you resign, get a written opinion from an employment or professional-conduct lawyer on:
- what you can and can't say to Tarvo and Kilima now
- whether the Tarvo work is firm-billed under firm engagement letters
- what confidential material you hold and how to handle it

**4. "Profitable by month 4" has no cash model behind it.** You've modelled billings, not cash. Kenyan corporate clients often pay 60 to 120+ days after invoice. Withholding tax on professional fees, VAT treatment, and the ramp in WIP all delay cash. A firm billing 1.36M a month can still be short on cash for many months.

**5. Some costs are missing.** Employer NSSF and housing levy, your own tax on drawings and LLP profit share, LSK and practising fees, PI insurance at proper cover levels, bookkeeping and accountancy, setup legal fees, equipment and fit-out, marketing, bank charges, and bad debt. A 10 to 15% contingency is normal for a first-year model.

**6. Savings are thin for the risk.** Six months of household expenses may not cover a firm that takes 9 to 12 months to reach cash break-even, plus your own income drop of roughly 38% (650k to 400k gross) and the loss of employer benefits. Plan for at least 12 months of runway that excludes your Tarvo assumption.

**7. The two precedents are informative.** The partner who closed within 18 months is the more relevant data point. Find out what made the difference: whether the successful one brought a portable client base, whether the failed one relied on a single client, and how each handled cash flow. Ask the one who closed what they wish they'd known.

## On your wife

She may not be risk averse so much as seeing the single-client dependency and the thin runway. Those are legitimate. Her view and the numbers point the same way, so it's worth treating her objection as data rather than as a difference in temperament.

## What I'd do before resigning

1. **Get the legal opinion** on the non-solicit clause and what you can do with clients now.
2. **Build a 12-month cash-flow model**, not a billings model, with 90-day collections, withholding tax, VAT, a realistic ramp, and a version where Tarvo pays nothing in year one.
3. **Get something signed.** A letter of intent or engagement with Tarvo, once the legal position allows, is worth far more than the goodwill.
4. **Ask the firm for the partnership timeline in writing.** "Two to three years" said three years ago is a warning sign. If they can't commit, that tells you something useful.
5. **Talk to an accountant** about LLP structure, tax on drawings, and withholding.
6. **Set a decision threshold.** For example: resign only when Tarvo has signed, the cash model survives the no-Tarvo case for 12 months, and the legal opinion is clean.

Your plan may well work, and the Tarvo relationship is a real asset. But right now the case depends on one client who hasn't committed and a cash position that hasn't been modelled. Those are fixable before March, and fixing them is what would make this a sound decision rather than a hopeful one.

strategy-07__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

Padhai's growth engine is now schools. The consumer app is still how we earn trust with students and parents, and it stays a brand asset and a funnel, but it stops being an independent growth bet in 2025.

## The shape that clicked

```
        Schools (140 partners, annual contracts, 81% GM)
          |                          |
   students use Padhai        teachers want state-board alignment
          |                          |
   parents trust the app   <-- the 2025 restructuring
          |
   paid subscriptions (31% of B2C paid came via a school)
          |
   direct B2C (CAC ₹780, ~9% monthly churn)
```

Your draft had two parallel engines, so the reader had to hold both at once. The data shows one engine and one feeder. Nearly a third of B2C paid users arrive through a school, so B2C is partly downstream of schools. The restructuring question also stops being a tie: state-board alignment is what school demand asks for, and vernacular content mainly helps the consumer funnel.

## What moved

- **Consumer story:** from "a consumer company at heart" to "the trust that schools buy." The founders' origin story stays, but it becomes the reason schools trust us.
- **Equal energy:** cut. The note makes one bet and says what waits.
- **Vernacular content:** from 2025 priority to deferred, because the content team can only do one restructuring.
- **₹199 tier:** moved to "not in 2025" until the B2C unit economics improve. At ₹780 CAC and ~9% churn, a cheaper tier makes the math harder.
- **Missing:** the state-board demand numbers, the school-acquired churn rate, and the ₹199 tier economics.

## Rebuilt

**Where Padhai goes in 2025**

**The decision.** Padhai is becoming a school-led business. Schools are where our growth and margin are, and they are where the consumer business gets its best users. Our consumer app remains the way we earn parent and student trust. We stop treating direct-to-consumer as a separate growth engine.

**What the consumer business proved.** 1.2M registered learners and 86k paid subscriptions mean parents trust Padhai. That trust is the reason schools sign with us, and it is still the asset we are building on. Our brand is not a moat we can lean on alone; it's the thing schools buy.

**Why this, and why now.**
- Schools: 140 partners, ₹3.4 Cr ARR, 81% gross margin, annual contracts. Expansion into chains is where the economics compound.
- Direct B2C: CAC rose from ₹410 to ₹780 in 18 months, and paid churn is about 9% monthly. Growing it alone gets more expensive each year.
- 31% of B2C paid users were acquired through a school. Schools already feed the consumer side.
- Our content team of 14 can deliver one major restructuring in 2025. Teachers and schools are asking for state-board alignment, so that is the one we will do.

**What we will do in 2025.**
1. Ship state-board alignment for [named boards], led by school demand.
2. Build teacher dashboards on top of it so schools can run Padhai across classes and chains.
3. Keep parent progress reports as the bridge between school and home [confirm these can ship without content restructuring].
4. Keep the consumer app running as a funnel and trust layer, with no new paid acquisition spend beyond [budget].

**What waits.**
- Vernacular content (Kannada, Tamil, Hindi): planned for [2026 / after state-board work], to be prioritized by school and region demand.
- The ₹199/month tier: not launched until B2C CAC and churn reach [target] or the tier is shown to work without new content.

**What would change this.** If school renewals fall, or if school-acquired paid users churn much faster than direct ones, we revisit the split. We'll review both numbers at [date].

---

**Before this goes to the offsite, you'll need:**
- Which state boards the 140 schools and the pipeline ask for, and how many schools each one covers. This decides whether state-board alignment is the right restructuring.
- Churn for school-acquired paid users versus direct users. If school users churn much less, the case gets stronger.
- Renewal and expansion rates for schools, to back up the "compounds" claim.
- Tier-2 demand: whether the schools you want next are in the regions that need vernacular content. This may make the vernacular case later, not dead.
- The ₹199 tier's unit economics, so you can say what would have to be true to launch it.

**For the founders:** you can say "the consumer business built the trust, and schools are how we turn that trust into a business." It keeps their story and makes the decision follow from it.

team-05__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine
Coordinators are leaving an unsustainable role. Caseload nearly doubled, the support that made it manageable was removed, and the pay gap made leaving easy. Pay is part of the fix, not the whole of it.

## The shape that clicked

```
Caseload 25 -> 45 ----+
Supervision lost -----+
Holiday club cover ---+--> role unsustainable --> resignation
Isolation ------------+            ^
                                   |
                      pay gap makes leaving affordable
```

The paper leads with pay, but only one of four leavers raised it, and the other three described workload and isolation. A pay-only proposal leaves caseload at 45, so the next resignation is likely. The trustee will spot that gap.

## What moved
- **Pay**: from lead argument -> to one of several linked fixes, because the evidence supports that framing.
- **Other factors**: from a closing sentence -> to the core evidence, because they explain the resignations.
- **"Continue to monitor"**: cut, because it is not a proposal. Replace it with a review date.
- **Cost**: recheck before Thursday. £3,100 × 7 posts = £21,700 exactly, which suggests this is salary only and omits on-costs. It also does not say whether the four vacant posts are costed at £26,500.
- **Missing**: (a) a sourced sector comparison for £23,400; (b) what the caseload fix costs; (c) the cost of turnover (recruitment, training, paused schemes); (d) whether the designated reserve can fund a recurring cost.

## Rebuilt

**Volunteer Coordinator Retention: Paper for Trustees**

**Summary**
Four of our seven Volunteer Coordinators have resigned since March. This has left 180 volunteers across Gateshead, Sunderland and South Tyneside without a dedicated contact, and the Reading Buddies scheme is paused in two schools.

**What leavers told us**
- Caseload rose from about 25 to 45 volunteers per coordinator after the 2023 restructure.
- The weekly peer supervision was lost when the Volunteer Manager post was frozen.
- Two coordinators described school holiday club cover as "the final straw".
- Three of the four described feeling isolated.
- One leaver was moving to a role paying £27,000 at a housing association. Our coordinator salary is £23,400, and [sector comparison and source to be added].

We read this as a role that became unsustainable, with pay making it easier to leave. A pay increase alone would not address the caseload, which is the main reason coordinators gave.

**Recommendations**
1. **Restore peer supervision** for coordinators: [cost and delivery route].
2. **Review caseload** against the 25-volunteer level before the 2023 restructure: [options and cost], with a report back to trustees by [date].
3. **Clarify holiday club cover**: [who covers, how it is staffed].
4. **Uplift coordinator pay to £26,500**, costing £[recalculated figure, including on-costs, and treatment of vacant posts] a year.

**Funding**
Pay and caseload costs recur. Trustees should decide whether these come from [recurring income] rather than the workforce development reserve, which is one-off.

**Cost of turnover**
Four resignations have cost us [recruitment, training and paused-service costs], in addition to the impact on 180 volunteers.

**Decision requested**
Trustees are asked to approve items 1 and 4 now, and to commission the caseload review in item 2 with a report by [date].

team-07__base.text:
## Bottom line for the call

**"The app is mostly failing at the till, not in the marketing. I'm asking you to pull the firmware fix forward from Q1 and approve three smaller actions now."**

Your draft listed four fixes with equal weight, so the room couldn't tell what mattered most. The data ranks them, and your talk track should too.

## Talk track (about 5 min)

**1. Where we are (30 sec)**
"We launched 2 September, targeting 25% of transactions scanned by end of October. We're at 6.2% across the region."

**2. Why (2 min)**
"Three things explain most of the gap, in order of impact:

- **The scanner fails on many phones.** 22 of our 38 stores run old POS firmware that can't read the app QR code on some Android devices. Customers try, it fails, and they give up. Stores on the new firmware scan at 11.8%. Stores on the old firmware scan at 2.9%. That's the biggest single factor in the data.
- **Customers don't know about it.** 38% of surveyed customers said they didn't know the app existed. Training was a 20-minute video and only about half of staff watched it. Posters arrived late in about 10 stores.
- **Staff stopped offering it.** When scans fail in front of customers, cashiers feel embarrassed and quit pitching it. A failed scan hurts the staff's confidence as well as the customer's experience.

Points value is a possible factor, but it's the weakest signal. Only 22% said they're not interested, and the sample doesn't isolate points as the cause."

**3. What I'm asking for (1.5 min)**
"Four decisions:

1. **Pull the firmware rollout for the 22 old-firmware stores forward** from Q1 to [date]. This is the one that moves the numbers. I'd like IT to confirm the timeline and any blockers by [date].
2. **Interim workaround for those 22 stores until the firmware is updated:** [e.g., a manual loyalty-number lookup at the till, to be confirmed with IT]. This stops customers hitting a dead end.
3. **Replace the 20-minute video with a 5-minute in-store huddle** run by store managers, plus a short floor reference card. Target: all staff briefed within two weeks.
4. **Make sure every store has posters by [date],** with a check in the stores that were late.

I'm **not** asking to change points values yet. We should measure again after firmware and training are fixed, then decide whether points need work."

**4. What to expect (1 min)**
"Honest caveat: even if all 22 stores reached the 11.8% we see in the upgraded stores, the region would land around 12%, not 25%. Firmware is necessary but not sufficient. Training and awareness are what get us from 12% toward the target, which is why I'm asking for all of it, in that order."

## Likely questions

- **"Why not just do everything?"** Firmware is the only fix with a clear, large effect and a fixed dependency on IT. Training and posters are cheap and can run in parallel, but the firmware date is the one that controls the timeline.
- **"Is the firmware really the cause?"** The comparison is not a controlled test. New-firmware stores may differ in other ways. The gap (11.8% vs 2.9%) and the customer complaints about failed scans both point the same way, so I'd treat it as the strongest lead, not proof. We can confirm by piloting the workaround in a few stores.
- **"What does the firmware upgrade cost?"** [Fill in from IT.]

## Before the call

- Fill in the brackets (dates, IT's cost and timeline, workaround feasibility).
- Ask IT tonight whether the manual lookup is actually possible. If it isn't, cut point 2 rather than promise it.
- Keep the talk track to the four asks. If you have time, put the data in a one-page appendix rather than the main talk.

positioning-09__base.text:
**Suggested English introduction (about 170 words):**

> **Welcome to Ryokan Shiraume**
>
> For five generations, since 1912, our family has run this ryokan in the same town, beside the same hot spring. We have only six rooms, so every guest receives our full attention. Each room has its own private outdoor bath (rotenburo) filled with hot spring water, so you will never need to share a bath. Guests with tattoos are completely welcome.
>
> In winter, our dinners feature snow crab from the fishing port just 400 metres away. My husband buys it at the morning auction. Our kaiseki follows the seasons, and we can prepare vegetarian kaiseki if you let us know three days before your stay.
>
> We are two hours from Kyoto by train, and we collect guests from the station free of charge. Please write to us with any questions. Many of our guests remember my mother-in-law, who serves tea with great care at the age of 88.

**Advice on homepage order:**

1. **Opening statement.** Lead with what makes you different: six rooms and a private bath in each. Visitors comparing large hotels will see this immediately. Drop generic phrases like "unforgettable memories," since every hotel uses them.

2. **Your story.** The five generations since 1912 build trust quickly. Place it right after the opening, with a photo of the building or family if you have one.

3. **Reassurance for worried guests.** Put the tattoo policy and the access information (2 hours from Kyoto, free station pickup) high on the page, not buried in a FAQ. These are the questions that stop bookings. Since about one in four foreign guests asks about tattoos, answering before they ask saves emails and builds confidence.

4. **Food.** Snow crab (November to March) and the vegetarian option with three days' notice come next. Seasonal specifics are more appealing than the word "kaiseki" alone.

5. **Room list.** Once guests trust you, they will look at rooms.

6. **Detailed access information.** Directions and timetables belong here, for guests who have already decided to come.

7. **Your mother-in-law.** She is a wonderful part of your story, but she works better on an "About us" or "Our family" page with a photo, rather than in the homepage introduction. Reviews that mention her will also bring her to guests' attention naturally.

Finally, read your text aloud and ask whether any sentence could appear on a competitor's website. If it could, replace it with a specific fact from your ryokan, as I have done above.

proposal-01__base.text:
**Rewritten Statement of Need and Impact** (about 340 words)

When labour begins in the villages outside Kisumu, many women face a choice no one should have to make: stay home and hope, or find transport to a facility that is distant, costly, and often intimidating. [Insert the current county figure on facility births or maternal mortality, with its source.]

Mama Salama Trust was founded in 2011 by retired midwives who believed the answer lay in trust. Today, 41 community health promoters work across 19 sub-locations, in partnership with the County Department of Health since 2019. Our model respects local birthing traditions while steadily connecting women to skilled facility care.

In 2022 we added two elements. A mobile-money transport voucher (KES 600 per trip) lets women in labour reach a facility by boda boda, so cost no longer decides whether they go. Promoters also began using a simple danger-signs checklist at 32 and 36 weeks, so warning signs are caught before labour begins. Early uptake was slowed by network failures. Switching providers resolved the problem, and uptake grew.

The results from January 2022 to December 2023 are clear. Among enrolled women, facility births rose from 54% to 88%. In comparison sub-locations without vouchers, the rate moved only from 51% to 59%. We recorded no maternal deaths among 1,312 enrolled women, compared with four in the comparison area.

Demand has followed the results. The County Government has asked us to extend the program to Nyando sub-county.

We request KES 18.4 million over two years to extend the program to 12 additional sub-locations, sustain promoter stipends, and commission an independent external evaluation, so that what works in these villages can be verified and replicated.

---

**On ordering:** I moved from chronology to a problem-solution-evidence-ask structure. Opening with the stakes for women gives reviewers a reason to care before they see the organisation's history. The history is compressed into a single paragraph that establishes credibility. The results come before the ask, so the funding request follows from the evidence.

**Two things to check before submitting:**

1. **The maternal death comparison is the weakest claim.** Zero versus four deaths is too small a number to show statistical significance, and "approx. 1,100" is imprecise. I stated the figures plainly without overclaiming. Reviewers who know public health will notice the small numbers, so consider acknowledging the limitation explicitly and pointing to the external evaluation as the way to test it rigorously. That turns a possible weakness into evidence of rigour.

2. **Add a local need statistic.** The opening needs a Kisumu-specific figure with a source. Without it, the need is asserted rather than shown, and that is probably the most persuasive upgrade you can make.

pitch-03__base.text:
**Rewrite:**

Subject: Rostering review, and a pilot result you may find useful

Dear Ms Okafor,

Daniel Ferris suggested I contact you as the Trust reviews its rostering approach ahead of next year.

In a six-month pilot at a 900-bed Midlands acute trust, ShiftWell wards cut agency nurse spend by £312,000, reduced bank shift requests by 22%, and brought unfilled night shifts down from 9% to 3%.

Would a 30-minute call be worth your time to see whether similar results are realistic for [Trust name]? I can send the pilot methodology beforehand.

Kind regards,
Priya Nair
Account Executive, ShiftWell

**What I changed and why:**

- **Subject line:** The original was a generic topic line that could be sent to anyone. The new one references the rostering review and promises something specific.
- **Cut the adjectives:** "Industry-leading," "cutting-edge," "unprecedented challenges," and "smarter rosters" are what made it sound like every other vendor. A numbers-driven reader skips them.
- **Removed claims you can't back up yet:** "Fully compliant with NHS data standards" invites a question you'd need to answer with evidence (e.g. DSPT or DTAC status). Add it back only with documentation.
- **Led with your strongest evidence:** The pilot results were buried in the middle. They're now the core of the email.
- **Specific outcomes, not a survey score:** The rise in "my rota lets me plan my life" from 31% to 58% is compelling but softer and more open to challenge. Save it for the follow-up or the demo.
- **Offered the methodology:** For someone who'll scrutinise the numbers, offering how the pilot was measured builds credibility faster than more claims.
- **Clearer ask:** A 30-minute call with a specific purpose is easier to say yes to than a vague "would you be available for a demo."

**Before you send, check:**

- Do you have permission to cite the pilot Trust, even anonymised? If not, say "a 900-bed acute trust" and keep the figures.
- Is the £312,000 figure for a defined period? Be ready to say what it covers, since a numbers person will ask.
- Can you actually send the methodology? If not, change that line so you don't promise it.
- Was the pilot controlled? If not, avoid implying that ShiftWell alone caused all the changes. Something like "wards using ShiftWell saw..." is accurate and safer.
