- **Diversions**: we have sent 17 patients to other hospitals since January, with occupancy averaging 91%. [Add revenue lost per diverted patient: P___.]

Current overtime and turnover together run about P4.4M a year, more than twice the cost of the four positions. I expect overtime to fall substantially once these positions are filled. I will confirm this against the roster [and attach it].

Two nurses have told me they are applying abroad. The timing matters: filling these positions now protects the staff we have.

If four positions are not approved, I propose a six-nurse float pool across ICU, ER and step-down, with a written commitment that at least [X] night shifts per week are ICU-only and that I report the ICU night ratio to you monthly.

I am available this week to walk through the roster and the cost figures.

Respectfully,
[Name]
ICU Nurse Manager

Attachments: staffing roster (Jan–Jun), overtime summary, incident reports (9 night-shift events)

business-decision-05__base.text:
I'd go with option 3, but as a counter-offer you put in writing before Friday, not a quiet hope they'll say yes.

**Why**

- **NSW is the problem, not VIC.** It's 12% of your volume and 40% of your time, with freight costs, a flaky wholesaler, and late payments. Handing NSW to a distributor fixes the thing that's draining you. Keeping VIC keeps your best margin and the relationships your venues value. Jess knowing everyone is an asset a 3-year exclusive would throw away.
- **The exclusive is the risky part.** Coastline dropped two craft brands after 18 months. A 3-year exclusive across VIC and NSW means you can't back out if they deprioritise you, and you'd be locked out of your own market. "Exclusive is how we do it" softening on the second call suggests it's negotiable.
- **The $140k fermenter bet depends on volume you don't have yet.** Your cash is $210k. Spending most of it on tanks against a distributor's projections, without a committed minimum, is how a small brewery gets squeezed. Don't commit capex until volume is proven.
- **Option 4 isn't free.** Six months of waiting means your NSW problems continue and you lose the chance to negotiate from a position where Coastline wants you.
- **Raff's "now or never" is a pressure line.** Good distribution deals don't expire in a week. Ask him what specifically disappears if you say no to exclusivity.

**What to put to Coastline by Friday**

- NSW only, non-exclusive or exclusive for NSW only.
- Performance terms: volume minimums with an exit right if they miss them for two consecutive quarters.
- A clause letting you terminate if they drop or de-list a brand without notice.
- No capex obligation on your side without a written volume commitment.
- Payment terms that fix your late-payment problem, with a clear remedy.
- Put the "150+ venues" claim into the contract as a target, not a promise, or get named accounts.

**Hedge with Ironbark**

Call them this week. Test whether they'd take NSW alone on similar terms. That gives you a real alternative, which is what makes the Coastline counter credible. If Coastline refuses any non-exclusive or performance-linked structure, that tells you most of what you need to know, and you go with Ironbark on NSW or stay self-distributed there.

**Caveats**

I don't know the per-HL margin difference between NSW and VIC after freight, or what the 28% actually comes out to in dollars, so run those numbers before you sign anything. And if your NSW volume is shrinking or the wholesaler is about to fail, that changes the urgency.

If Coastline says yes to NSW-only with reasonable terms, you're done and it's a good outcome. If they say no, you've still learned they'd rather have all of your market than the part you actually need help with.

academic-05__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

Letters stopped being a way to pay for life in Boston and became a way to stay part of Kilbrack, and the turn comes around 1895, not 1890 or 1900.

## The shape that clicked

```
1880 ------------------- 1895 ------------------- 1910
 | OBLIGATION               | BELONGING                 |
 | money in 71% of letters  | money in 23%              |
 | work, passage, debts     | longer letters, feeling,  |
 |                          | memories of named places  |
 |-----------------religion runs through both------------|
 |--marriage advice: two writers, one family, flagged----|
```

Neither option fits your data. Chronological splits at 1890 and 1900, but your break is at 1895. Thematic separates money from belonging, when your hunch is that the two are one shift: the money obligation ends, and the letters take on a new job. The 1895 break carries the argument, so the structure should follow it.

## What moved

- Your 3.1 and 3.2 boundaries: 1880–1890 and 1890–1900 become 1880–1895 and 1895–1910, because the money drop is the evidence for the break.
- Money material: from a standalone theme into the obligation section, where it explains the early letters.
- Religion: from a standalone theme into a thread that runs through both sections, because it shows the parish continuity that makes the shift visible.
- Marriage advice: from a standalone theme into a flagged thread, because the two-writer family could be a quirk. Keep it as a caveat or case study, not as a pillar.
- Your hunch: from unwritten to the argument of 3.2, which needs quoted letters behind it.
- Cut: nothing from the existing 6,000 words is lost. Most of it is description and can be recut under these headings.
- Missing: the number of letters per period across all four collections, and whether the money drop holds in every collection or mainly in the Ó Ceallaigh letters. [per-period counts needed]

## Rebuilt

**Chapter 3: From remittance to belonging, 1880–1910**

**3.1 Obligation: letters as payment, 1880–1895**
Open with the claim that early letters are mostly accounts: passage tickets, debts, remittances. Use the Ó Ceallaigh letters as the core case. [Money share by collection, 1880–1895]

**3.2 Belonging: letters as connection, 1895–1910**
Open with the shift: after about 1895, money nearly disappears (71% to 23%) and letters lengthen and turn to feeling, homesickness and specific Kilbrack places. Argue your hunch here, in the writers' own words, and show that the money obligation ending is what frees the letters for this. [Quoted examples with letter IDs]

**3.3 Threads across both periods**
- *Religion:* steady throughout, so it shows what stayed constant while the letters changed.
- *Marriage advice:* framed as tentative, with the two-writer family named as a limitation or case study.

**Recommendation:** Use this structure. The 1895 break is what your evidence supports, and it lets your descriptive material serve an argument. Before writing, check the per-period counts and the collection breakdown. If the drop holds across all four collections, the spine is secure.

strategy-06__base.text:
Your colleague is right. The current order makes readers wait for the argument. Lead with the conclusion, then let each section support it.

## Proposed structure

**Page 1: Summary and decisions**
- The 2025 thesis in two or three sentences
- The evidence behind it
- The resourcing decision you need from the exec team
- The main risks

**Page 2: Why this direction**
- Market context, framed as the problem each theme answers

**Page 3: What we've proven**
- 2024 achievements, with the dynamic slotting pilot as the lead item

**Pages 4-5: Themes and resourcing**
- Each theme with its goal, its evidence, and its dependencies
- The allocation, with reasons

**Page 6: Risks, dependencies, and what would change the plan**

## Draft page 1

> In 2025 we should make dynamic slotting our primary growth bet, and build the platform reliability and carrier experience work it depends on. Pilot results show a 31% reduction in truck dwell time and €38k per site per quarter in demurrage savings for customers. Both pilot customers want it extended to five more sites, and three prospects have asked for demos. We are asking the exec team to endorse this prioritisation. France and analytics remain on the roadmap but are sequenced behind external dependencies: a local partner and the data warehouse migration.

Then list the decisions: (1) endorse dynamic slotting as the priority theme, (2) approve the tiered allocation below, (3) approve France discovery work conditional on partner identification.

## On "roughly equally"

I don't think it's defensible, and you're right to question it. Equal allocation signals that you have no priority, and it doesn't match the dependencies:

- Analytics and France can't absorb full-time effort yet. Analytics is blocked by the migration, and France can't proceed without a partner. Equal allocation would leave those people waiting or doing low-value work.
- Dynamic slotting has the strongest evidence and clearest demand. Concentrating effort there is where the return is.

You can respect each sponsor without equal shares. Give each theme a defined outcome and a minimum commitment, and let the amount of effort follow the evidence and the dependencies. For example, using illustrative figures to replace with your actual capacity:

| Theme | Illustrative share | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Dynamic slotting | 35-40% | Proven outcome, customer pull, 7 sites to deliver |
| Platform reliability | 20% | Prerequisite for scaling slotting; P1 incidents still matter |
| Carrier experience | 20% | Carriers increasingly require slot booking; builds on portal v2 |
| Analytics | 10-15%, gated | Starts in earnest when the migration completes |
| France | 5-10%, discovery only | Scales once a partner is signed |

Before the exec read, talk to each internal sponsor. Show them their theme's outcome, minimum commitment, and what would trigger more investment. Most sponsors object less to a lower share than to being unsure where they stand.

## Caveats to address before the board reads it

Investors will test the evidence, so pre-empt these:

- **Sample size.** Two sites over ten weeks, both in Venlo. Say this plainly, and state what you'll measure in the 7-site rollout to test whether the result generalises.
- **Whose money it is.** The €38k in demurrage savings accrues to customers, not Havenlijn. The board will ask how it turns into revenue through pricing, expansion, or retention. Add a line on this. If the 7 sites held the pilot effect, the customer savings would be roughly €1M a year, which is a strong retention argument, but it needs to be stated as an assumption.
- **Demand signals.** Extension requests and demo requests are encouraging, not pipeline. Report them as such, or convert them into a number of signed commitments before the presentation if you can.
- **Reliability as a dependency.** If slotting scales on the same platform, reliability work is part of the slotting case, not a separate theme. Saying so makes the allocation easier to defend.

If you share the capacity figures or the sponsor list, I can draft the full theme pages and the allocation rationale.

team-10__base.text:
Your instinct is right. The report's own analysis points to a different primary cause than the recommendation addresses, and council staff or a budget analyst will probably spot it.

**What's not clicking**

1. **The data points at completeness, not capacity.** Returned applications take 104 days versus 31 for complete ones, and each returned application cycles back 2.3 times and re-enters at the back of the queue. Rework may be a large share of the 412-application queue and of reviewer time. Adding reviewers without reducing returns means paying to process the same rework faster.

2. **The staffing math doesn't reach 6.** Volume rose 18% against flat 9 FTE. At constant productivity, that's roughly 1.6 FTE of gap (9 × 1.18 ≈ 10.6). Six positions is about 67% more capacity. The report doesn't explain how it got from a 1.6-FTE gap to 6, and the rework load would have to be quantified to justify the difference.

3. **Cedar Falls is evidence for the other recommendation.** A 40% drop in returns from pre-application checks is the most directly relevant result in the report, and it's presented without being connected to the recommendation.

**Check these before you raise it**

- Is "40% drop in returns" a relative reduction (61% → ~37%) or a 40-percentage-point drop? The difference matters.
- Is the 300-application sample random, and does it cover the full year?
- Does the 104-day vs. 31-day gap reflect the returns themselves, or are complex projects both more likely to be returned and slower regardless? Some of the gap is probably confounding.
- Can you estimate reviewer hours spent on resubmissions versus first reviews? That single number could carry the whole argument.

**How to raise it without undermining your boss**

Go to your department head privately, before the report circulates. Frame it as protecting the recommendation, not challenging it: "Council will likely ask why 6 positions and not a completeness fix, since our own data points there. I'd like us to answer that question in the report before they ask it." Bring the data and the questions above. Most department heads would rather hear this from staff than from a council member.

Then offer options rather than a replacement recommendation:

- **Keep the 6 positions but add a completeness component** (pre-application checklist, plan-check templates, or a Cedar Falls-style pilot), with metrics and a 12-month check-in.
- **Phase the request**, e.g., 2–3 positions now plus a completeness initiative, with a return request if targets aren't met.
- **Present alternatives considered.** A short section showing the options and tradeoffs makes the recommendation stronger, not weaker.

**Sample language you could propose**

> *Analysis note:* Application returns for incompleteness are the largest identified driver of processing time, and each return re-enters the queue at the back. Neighboring Cedar Falls reported a 40% reduction in returns following pre-application completeness checks. Staff recommends pursuing completeness improvements in parallel with capacity additions, and has quantified reviewer hours consumed by resubmissions to inform the staffing level requested.

If your boss won't change the recommendation, you can still make the analysis section accurate. Council is better served by a report that shows its reasoning, and that protects you if the numbers are challenged later. If the disconnect is still there after that conversation, you've done your part by making it visible.

team-10__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

Most of the delay comes from applications being sent back, so the report should lead with intake quality, and the six positions should be presented as the second lever, backed by data we don't yet have.

## The shape that clicked

```
New application -> Intake -> Complete? --yes--> Review -> Permit
                              |
                              no (61%)
                              v
                           Returned -> resubmit -> back of queue -> (more review load)
```

The current draft has the returns finding in Analysis but recommends only headcount. Council will see that gap: if most applications come back incomplete, why would more reviewers be the first fix? Reviewers also process the resubmissions, so six new positions are sized against inflow the department partly generates itself.

## What moved

- **Returns finding:** moved to the top of Analysis, since it explains most of the 79-day average (183 returned applications at 104 days plus 117 complete ones at 31 days works out to roughly the reported average).
- **Staffing claim:** kept, but now tied to a measurement. The draft doesn't separate queue wait from review time, so it can't show that capacity is the binding constraint.
- **Recommendation:** expanded from one action to two, with the six positions still included. This supports your department head's request rather than replacing it.
- **Cedar Falls figure:** kept, attributed as their report, and flagged for local feasibility.
- **Missing:** the items in brackets below.

**Handling your boss:** raise this with them before the draft goes to council. Frame it as "the data shows returns are the main driver, and adding an intake fix makes our staffing request easier to defend." The recommendation wording is their call; the draft is written so they can keep the six positions as requested or phase them.

## Rebuilt

**Background**
The average time from application to permit issuance for residential projects rose from 34 days (2021) to 79 days (2024). There are currently 412 applications in the queue. The Home Builders Association has submitted a formal letter of concern.

**Analysis**
Staff reviewed a sample of 300 applications closed in 2024. Of these, 61% were returned at least once as incomplete, most often for missing structural calculations, site plans not to scale, or missing energy compliance forms. Returned applications took an average of 104 days to permit, compared with 31 days for applications complete on first submission. Returned applications averaged 2.3 resubmissions, and each one re-entered the back of the queue.

Returned applications account for most of the increase in average processing time. [Staff to confirm: how many of the 412 current applications are resubmissions.]

Review capacity is also a factor. Plan review staffing has been flat at 9 FTE since 2019, while application volume rose 18%. [Staff to add: average reviewer time per application, and the split of total wait between queue time and review time.]

Neighboring jurisdictions have introduced pre-application completeness checks. Cedar Falls reports a 40% reduction in returned applications after doing so. [Staff to confirm whether a comparable check is feasible here.]

**Recommendation**
Staff recommends two actions:

1. Introduce a pre-application completeness check and standard submittal checklist to reduce incomplete first submissions. [Cost and timeline to be added.]
2. Authorize six additional Plan Reviewer positions (approx. $720,000/yr loaded) to address review capacity, with reporting on queue time, return rate, and time to permit at 6 and 12 months.

**Before this goes to council, check:**
- The sample covers only applications closed in 2024. Applications still stuck in the queue aren't in it, so the delay may be understated. Say so.
- Confirm whether the sample is residential only, matching the 34-to-79-day figure.

proposal-03__base.text:
I'd lead with your own history, not the vendor stat. The Dayton outage, the $48k penalty, and the insurer's letter are specific, verifiable, and already cost you money. A CFO can't dismiss those as a pitch. The 60% figure is vendor-sourced, and "Gartner-ish" will invite the question "which is it?" If you keep it at all, put it in an appendix with the real source.

**Reorganized outline**

1. **The ask (one slide):** $340k for cloud migration, 6 months, phased by site. Give the recommendation and the decision needed up front.
2. **What's already costing us:** 3 unplanned outages, 31 hours, $48k SLA penalties to Brennan Foods, ~$11k overtime. That's roughly $59k in direct costs last year, before any lost business.
3. **Risks we're carrying:**
   - Ridgeline Mutual's written 18% premium increase (~$22k/yr) unless we have offsite backup with tested restore
   - 7-year-old hardware
   - Key-person risk: the person who built the config has retired, and nobody fully understands it
4. **Options considered:** This slide is what most separates a business case from a pitch. Compare:
   - A. Status quo plus break/fix
   - B. Offsite backup/DR only (likely cheapest, probably satisfies the insurer)
   - C. Full cloud migration ($340k)
   
   For each, show cost, what problems it solves, and what it leaves open.
5. **Recommendation and financials:** Break down the $340k, and show the recurring cloud cost versus today's run-rate. Show payback with the assumptions stated.
6. **Benefits, tied to the problems above:** Scalability and modern tools matter, but connect them to specific pain points. Remote dispatch access and DR improvements should map to the outages.
7. **Timeline and risk:** Document the current config before anything moves. Explain the phasing, rollback plan, and which site goes first.
8. **Decision requested**

**Be ready for these CFO questions**

- What's the recurring cost after year one, versus what we pay now?
- Why not Option B? If backup satisfies the insurer for much less, why spend $340k?
- What's the payback period, and how much of the ~$81k/yr in avoidable costs (insurance plus last year's outage costs) is repeatable?
- What happens if the migration slips or a site fails mid-move?

**Honest take:** Your case may be weaker on pure dollars than it feels. If the recurring cloud costs are high, Option B might win financially, and migration could be justified only by scalability and the key-person risk. Presenting Option B as a real alternative will make your recommendation more credible, even if she ends up choosing it. Run the numbers on recurring costs before Thursday, because that's the first thing she'll check.

If you share the vendor's pricing for the recurring portion and a rough estimate of the backup-only option, I can help you build the comparison table.

proposal-04__base.text:
The panel's question has a fairly clear answer, and it points to a design you already have. **Your strongest asset is the 18 shared sites.** The overlap is not a nuisance. It is the basis for one study.

## 1. A candidate central question

> *Do field-margin management regimes increase wild bee nesting in agricultural landscapes, and does pesticide exposure offset those gains?*

Or, more compactly: **Does margin management support wild bees when they are also exposed to agrochemicals?**

WP1 measures the benefit of management, WP2 measures the exposure, and the shared sites let you test whether the benefit survives the exposure. That is one question with a testable interaction, not three projects.

## 2. Check the design against the question

Before you rewrite, look at two problems the panel may already sense:

- **Different guilds.** WP1 studies ground-nesting bees; *Osmia bicornis* is a cavity nester. The shared sites link the studies by location, not by species. Say so explicitly and justify the link: either the study is about landscape-level exposure of the wider community, or you need a second measure of exposure relevant to ground nesters (e.g., soil or floral residues).
- **Spatial scale.** Pollen loads reflect foraging ranges of hundreds of metres, not the margin itself. Residues in *Osmia* pollen characterise the surrounding landscape, so the exposure variable is landscape-scale while your management variable is margin-scale. Either show that the scales align, or add landscape context (land use within a set radius) as a covariate. This is the most likely methodological objection from reviewers.

## 3. What to do with WP3

WP3 is the weakest fit. It is a tool development project with an engagement goal, and it does not inform the central question. I'd recommend **cutting it from the core aims** and either:

- (a) keeping a small, clearly separate public-engagement activity in the dissemination plan, or
- (b) reframing it only if the Hummelwacht network can collect data at your study sites in a way that adds to the central question (e.g., bumblebee abundance as a third response variable), which would also require validating the app on field conditions rather than the pilot's nine common species.

Cutting it frees time and budget for the parts that matter to the question. You say you are attached to all three, but a focused proposal from a capable junior group will score better than a broad one that looks fragmented.

## 4. The volunteer and farmer overlap

Yes, this matters, and it matters beyond WP3. Volunteers who are farmers or farm neighbours create issues:

- **Independence of data.** If volunteers identify bees in fields they manage or live beside, observer bias and motivated reporting become risks, especially if agri-environment payments depend on the results.
- **Conflict of interest.** Stakeholders in the scheme you are evaluating should not be the data source for evaluating it.
- **Ethics and consent.** Check whether your data governance covers volunteers' locations and their agricultural activities.

If you keep any volunteer component, state how you will separate volunteers from site management, and use them only as a supplementary, not primary, data source.

## 5. Suggested restructure

- **Core aim:** test whether margin management benefits wild bee nesting when pesticide exposure is taken into account.
- **WP1 (core):** nesting survey across the 40 margins, with management regime as the main factor.
- **WP2 (core):** pollen residue analysis at the 25 sites, with explicit landscape-scale exposure metrics.
- **Integration:** an analysis explicitly modelling the management × exposure interaction at the 18 shared sites, plus the remaining sites for power.
- **WP3:** removed from the core; optional engagement activity or a clearly marked future extension.

## 6. Caveats

The 2.3× difference comes from 12 margins, so present it as a pilot signal and do a power analysis for the full 40 sites. The 68% residue detection rate is encouraging but should be reported with detection limits and the number of compounds screened.

If you tell me the exact wording of the panel's criteria and your word limits, I can help draft the revised aims and the integrating paragraph.

academic-05__base.text:
Your notes already point toward an answer. Your strongest finding is the break around 1895, and your chronological split puts the boundary at 1900, which may be the wrong place. Here's how I'd weigh it.

**Option A (chronological)**
- *For:* It matches the change you've documented, and readers can follow the arc.
- *Against:* As drafted, the sections are labelled by decade, not by argument. Your 1895 break falls in the middle of 3.1, and the chapter risks reading as "what happened in each decade" rather than "what changed and why."

**Option B (thematic)**
- *For:* Money, religion, and marriage are clear categories, and each has a visible story.
- *Against:* Religion shows no change, so the section would be flat. Marriage advice rests mostly on two writers in one family, which is thin for a full section. And the money section would show the 1895 drop but not explain what replaced it, which is the interesting part.

**My recommendation: a hybrid, organised by the argument.** Your hunch is the chapter's real claim: once the money obligation faded, letters took on the work of maintaining belonging. That is a claim about change, so the structure should reflect the break:

- **3.1 (c.1880–1895): letters as obligation.** Money dominates. Religion appears as routine background.
- **3.2 (c.1895–1910): letters as belonging.** Feeling, memory of Kilbrack, and sustained interest in home. Religion stays constant here, and that continuity can be your evidence: the faith was a fixed point across the shift, so it becomes a thread rather than a separate topic.
- Marriage advice can sit within 3.2 as one expression of belonging, with the two-writer caveat stated.

This keeps the chronology your evidence supports, but organises each section by function, not by decade. Your 6,000 words of mixed description may already be close to this; the task might be reordering rather than rewriting.

## The spine

Your strongest evidence is the report project, but the statement opens with passion and only reaches the project in paragraph three. Lead with the project and let it argue for UX.

## The shape that clicked

```
Current:   passion -> teaching empathy -> PROJECT -> adjectives -> close
New:       PROJECT -> why this is UX -> empathy from teaching -> gap + placement -> what I bring
```

Your mentor's "backwards" most likely means this. You make claims about yourself, then offer proof, and the proof is the most persuasive part. The three adjectives ("organised, communicator, learner") are claims with nothing behind them, and the project already shows all three. The childhood floor plans are charming but read as identity rather than evidence, so I've kept them only as a short line.

## What moved

- **Report project**: from paragraph three to the opening, because it is the evidence the panel will remember.
- **"Why UX"**: from a claim in paragraph one to a conclusion drawn from the project, because the work itself shows you were doing UX.
- **Teaching and empathy**: moved after the project and tied to specific behaviour, so the empathy is shown rather than asserted.
- **"Organised, communicator, learner"**: cut, because the project demonstrates each one.
- **Childhood floor plans**: cut to one clause.
- **Certificate and Figma**: moved to a paragraph on your current gap, which makes the placement request concrete.
- **Cut**: "I am excited to begin this next chapter of my life," because it says nothing specific.
- **Missing**: the specific area of design you want to work in. I've left a placeholder. Brightline will want to know what you'll do with the placement, and naming it sharpens everything else.

## Rebuilt

Last year, teachers at my school were spending about 11 hours each term on reports, much of it copying data between three systems. I interviewed 14 colleagues about where they got stuck and mapped the process on butcher's paper. I then built a prototype in Google Sheets with dropdowns and auto-filled comment banks, and tested it in three rounds with our Year 3–6 team. After rollout to all 60 staff, average report time dropped to about 6.5 hours. The principal has asked me to present the approach to two other schools in our network.

That project was user experience design, even though I didn't have the name for it then. The valuable part wasn't the spreadsheet. It was finding out where people actually got stuck, testing a version with them, and changing it when they told me it wasn't working. That is the discipline I want Brightline to teach me, and I want to apply it to [the area of design you want to focus on].

My empathy comes from teaching. I work with 28 Year 5 students who learn differently, and I adjust in real time when a lesson isn't landing. I use the same skills with colleagues: noticing where someone hesitates, asking what they need, and adapting before a problem grows. As a child I spent hours rearranging my bedroom and drawing floor plans of imaginary houses, and I still feel the same pull toward making things work well for the people who use them.

I'm not starting from zero. I have completed the Google UX Certificate and am currently learning Figma. What I lack is practice on problems beyond my own school, with a team and real users. That is what I hope the placement will give me.

I would bring the same habits to the Brightline cohort: interviewing before designing, testing before rolling out, and presenting what I learned. I would welcome the chance to learn alongside the other fellows.

## The spine

Fix commercial losses first, because that is the cheapest route to cost recovery and it needs no tariff change. Introduce telescopic tariffs only after metering is in place and supply has improved, since a volumetric tariff cannot be billed on unmetered connections.

## The shape that clicked

```
Commercial losses (illegal connections, unmetered supply, billing errors)
   │  fix first, no tariff change
   ▼
Cost recovery rises (~48% per point 6 — recheck, see below)
   │  metering now exists
   ▼
Volumetric telescopic tariff with lifeline slab (Option c)
   │  tied to service hours
   ▼
Residents pay more because supply is regular (point 4)
```

The note treats the commercial losses as a side finding, but they are the first step in the recommended sequence. Option (c) is also recommended without a cost-recovery figure, and it cannot be billed until the losses are fixed. That gap is why the note does not go anywhere.

## What moved

- **Commercial losses (point 6):** moved from the back of the argument to the recommendation, because it is the cheapest lever and the only one that does not depend on residents paying more.
- **Option (c):** moved from the recommendation to a second phase, because it depends on metering and on service improvements.
- **Point 4 (willingness to pay):** moved next to the tariff section, because it is the condition under which any tariff rise is defensible.
- **Point 5 (20% hike):** moved to the options comparison, because it is the option most exposed to the 1.5-hour supply problem.
- **Cut:** the phrase "in line with national best practice" as a justification. Keep the case studies, but let them show what the telescopic design achieved, not carry the recommendation.

**Check before this goes up:** the 48% figure may be overstated. NRW is 42%, and about half of that is commercial, so roughly 21% of water supplied is lost commercially. Recovering it would add about 21 points of billed volume. Billed volume is about 58% of supply now, so billed volume rises by a factor of roughly 79/58, about 1.36. Applied to 31%, that gives about 42%, not 48%. The gap may come from collection efficiency gains, which the note does not mention. Confirm the assumption with the team, or state it explicitly.

**Missing:** the cost-recovery figure for option (c), and the metering coverage in the 11 corporations.

## Rebuilt note

**To:** Principal Secretary
**Subject:** Revising water tariffs in municipal corporations: recommended sequence

**Recommendation.** Reduce commercial losses first, through metering, action on illegal connections and billing corrections. Estimated cost recovery is about [48%, to be verified], with no change to tariffs. Once metering is in place and supply is more regular, introduce a volumetric telescopic tariff with a lifeline slab (Option c) in a second phase. A tariff rise should not come before supply improves: residents in Raghunathpur and Sitanagar said they would pay more if supply were regular, and supply is currently 1.5 hours on alternate days.

**Background.** The tariff structure was notified in 2009 and has not been revised. Cost recovery across the 11 municipal corporations averages 31%. Non-revenue water is 42%, roughly half of it commercial losses.

**Options.**

| Option | Cost recovery | Equity | Depends on |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Status quo | 31% | Unchanged | Nothing |
| (b) 20% across-the-board hike | ~37% | Regressive; hits lifeline users | Supply improving first |
| (c) Telescopic with lifeline | [to be computed] | Progressive | Metering, supply improvement |
| Loss reduction (no tariff change) | ~[42–48%, to be verified] | Neutral | Metering, enforcement |

**Sequence.** Phase 1: loss reduction and metering. Phase 2: telescopic tariff with lifeline, once metering covers [X%] of connections. Phase 3: review against supply hours.

**Evidence.** [Three case studies, as currently drafted.]

**Risks and open items.** Metering coverage in the 11 corporations is [not yet confirmed]. The cost-recovery figure for option (c) is [pending]. The 48% estimate assumes [collection efficiency gains, to be stated].

positioning-05__base.text:
The draft leads with the claim your prospects have already started to discount, and it hides the facts they're actually asking about. Your sales calls are good evidence here. Buyers who say they're "tired of AI promises" and then ask about installation time are telling you what to put first.

## Answers to your questions

**1. Remove the AI framing, or move it lower?**
Remove it from the headline and subheadline, and describe the technology accurately lower down. "AI-powered" over a threshold-plus-anomaly-detection system is a credibility problem with engineers and plant managers, who will ask what the AI does. It is also a compliance risk. Under UK CAP rules and the EU Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, capability claims must be substantiated, and "anticipates failures" and "continuously learns" are claims you would need to back with data. Describe the mechanism plainly: "Learns each machine's normal vibration signature and alerts on deviations." That is more persuasive to this audience, and it is defensible.

**2. What should lead?**
Lead with the outcome the buyer cares about (fewer unplanned stoppages) and the one thing that removes their objection (installation without downtime). In the pilot data, the two strongest facts are the 31% reduction in unplanned downtime and the 20-minute, no-stoppage install. Your prospects already named installation as a concern, so answer it above the fold.

**3. Is there a risk in being too modest?**
Less than you might think. Plant managers buy on evidence and risk reduction, and "modest" can read as "proven and simple" if you're specific. The bigger risk is the opposite: vague confidence with no numbers. Being precise is what makes the page feel credible. The one thing to avoid is letting "modest" slide into "generic." "Retrofit vibration monitoring" is a plain description. "Monitoring solution for smart manufacturing" is not.

## Claims to verify before publishing

- **"11 and 16 days before they would have occurred."** The counterfactual needs a basis. How was it established: teardown, inspection, the failure that followed when the bearing was left in service? If you can't document it, write "flagged two bearing faults 11 and 16 days before they were replaced" or similar.
- **"31% reduction."** State the baseline period, the comparison period, and whether other changes happened on the line during the nine months.
- **"No cabling required."** Check what power and connectivity the sensor actually uses (battery life, wireless range, gateway requirements). If there is a gateway or a network connection, say so. Prospects will find out, and an overclaim here will cost you trust.
- **"Integration with leading MES and SCADA."** Name the protocols (OPC UA, Modbus, MQTT, REST, etc.) and which systems have been tested.
- **"Under 20 minutes."** Confirm this across more than one installer or site, and say whether it applies to all machine types.

## Revised outline

**Hero**
- Headline (see options below)
- Subheadline: "VibraLink is a magnetic vibration and temperature sensor kit that retrofits onto existing machines in under 20 minutes, with no line stoppage and no new cabling. It alerts your team to bearing and drive faults before they cause unplanned downtime."
- Primary CTA: "Book a 20-minute technical call"
- Secondary CTA: "Download the pilot report"
- Image: a sensor installed on a real motor or gearbox, not a stock photo of a factory floor

**Problem strip (three short points)**
- Unplanned stoppages cost more than planned maintenance.
- Retrofitting legacy machines usually means cabling, IT projects, and planned shutdowns.
- Most monitoring tools need months of setup before they show value.

**How it works (three steps)**
1. **Mount.** Magnetic sensor, no cabling, no line stoppage. Show a short install video.
2. **Learn.** The system builds a baseline of each machine's normal vibration and temperature. State the baseline period.
3. **Alert.** Threshold alerts plus anomaly detection flag deviations to the dashboard, email, or your SCADA/MES. Explain what triggers an alert and how false alarms are handled.

**Proof**
- Pilot case study: corrugated packaging plant, Bielefeld, nine months. Include the 31% figure with its baseline, the two bearing cases with the verification method, and the install time observed.
- Consider a short quote from the plant's maintenance lead, if they agree.
- Add a line noting this was a German pilot, since your UK, Dutch, and Nordic buyers will want to know whether it transfers.

**Fits your plant**
- Supported sensor types and machine categories
- Integration: protocols and tested systems
- Data: where it is stored (EU hosting, if applicable), who owns it, and GDPR/NIS2 position
- Support model and response times

**Commercial clarity**
Your prospects asked about installation, not price, but plant managers will look for cost early and leave if they can't find it. Show it:
- "From €380 per sensor point. No licence fee in year one."
- Give GBP equivalents for the UK and state whether prices exclude VAT.
- Give an example: "A 10-point installation on three lines costs €X in year one."
- If you want to keep pricing off the page, provide a clear route to it, such as a calculator or a "request a quote" form that gives a range.

**FAQ**
- How long does installation take, and does it need a shutdown?
- What happens if a sensor fails or the battery runs low?
- How many false alarms should I expect, and how do I tune them?
- Does it work on my machines (gearboxes, pumps, motors, fans)?
- Who owns the data, and where is it stored?
- What is the minimum number of points to start?

**Final CTA**
Repeat the primary CTA, with a one-line reassurance such as "Installation questions answered in 20 minutes."

## Headline options

Keep "AI" out of these. Each one states an outcome or a fact.

1. **"Know which bearing will fail before it stops your line."**
2. **"Retrofit vibration monitoring in 20 minutes, without stopping production."**
3. **"Cut unplanned downtime on machines you already run."**
4. **"Vibration and temperature monitoring that installs without a shutdown."**
5. **"Catch bearing faults more than a week early. No cabling, no downtime."**

Option 5 is accurate to the pilot (11 and 16 days). Avoid "two weeks" or "weeks ahead" unless you have more cases to support it.

## Suggested next steps

- Verify the five claims above and adjust wording to match what you can document.
- Run the revised page against the current one in a two-week test, using the same traffic source, and track demo requests and the time visitors spend on the install section.
- Ask the two prospects who raised the AI objection what would have made them trust the page. Their answers will tell you more than general best practice.

team-06__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

The complaints come from three mismatches in how the arrangement was built. The labs use the instruments unequally but split costs equally, one 0.6 FTE technician serves both, and nobody above the two heads owns the whole arrangement. Each lab's grievance is a symptom of one of these, and the Dean is the only person who can change all three.

## The shape that clicked

```
 Use:        Geochem 70% ────────────────┐
                                         ≠  (mismatch)
 Cost:       Geochem 50% / Hydro 50%  ───┘
                  │
 Access:   shared sheet, no enforcement
                  │
 Capacity: one 0.6 FTE tech ── 41 days down
                  │
 Ownership: two heads, no decider ── mediation failed x2
```

The old framing put the problem between the two labs, so the chair kept mediating between them. The new framing puts it in the structure, which is the Dean's to change. This also answers "so what are you asking me for": three decisions with a date attached.

## What moved

- **Cost split:** moved from the opening position to a supporting point, because the mismatch between use and cost is the root of the Adeyemi/Lindqvist dispute.
- **Hydrology no-shows (1 in 5):** kept, but reframed as a booking-discipline problem with a fix. Including it stops the memo reading as one-sided.
- **Mass spec downtime:** reframed from "people wait" to "capacity", since 41 days waiting on one part-time technician is a staffing issue.
- **Core facility option:** moved from a footnote to the recommended path, with Chemistry as the test case.
- **Cut:** the detail on individual bookings and the blow-by-blow of the mediation attempts. Both invite the Dean to pick a side.
- **Missing:** Chemistry's outcome data (utilisation, cost recovery, complaints), a breakdown of the $68k contract, the replacement cost of Priya's role, the ARC application name, and usage data across more than one semester.

## Rebuilt

**To:** Dean [name]
**From:** [Name], Chair, School of Earth Sciences
**Date:** [date]
**Subject:** Shared analytical instruments: decisions needed before the February renewal

**Purpose**
I am asking you to make three decisions on the mass spectrometer and XRF arrangement before the service contract renews in February.

**The problem**
The instruments were shared between Geochemistry and Hydrology after the 2021 merger, on the assumption of roughly equal use and equal cost. Neither holds. Geochemistry uses about 70% of instrument hours and Hydrology about 30%, but the merger agreement splits costs 50/50. Hydrology therefore carries more cost than its use justifies, and this gap underlies the friction between the two labs.

Three structural issues compound it:
- **Booking:** Bookings run on a shared spreadsheet with no enforcement, so entries are overwritten. About one in five Hydrology bookings went unused last semester. This needs a fix on both sides.
- **Capacity:** Both instruments depend on one 0.6 FTE technician split across two labs. The mass spectrometer was down 41 days last year, mostly waiting for her availability. This is a staffing constraint, not a behavioural one.
- **Ownership:** No one has authority over the arrangement as a whole. Two mediation attempts between the heads have not resolved it.

**Impact**
Three HDR students have had submission delayed in part by instrument access. An ARC reviewer flagged access to infrastructure as a weakness in [application]. The technician is considering other roles, and losing her would leave the mass spectrometer with no trained support.

**Why this needs your decision**
The cost allocation is set by the merger agreement, and the technician's time is shared across two labs. Changing either is above the school's authority.

**Options**
1. **Status quo with booking rules.** Low cost. Does not address the cost gap or capacity.
2. **Re-base costs on usage and add technical capacity.** Cost: [TBC]. Addresses the gap, but keeps the shared-governance problem.
3. **Move both instruments to a faculty-level core facility,** as Chemistry did in 2022. Chemistry's outcomes so far: [attach data]. Resolves cost, capacity and ownership together. Transition cost and timeline: [TBC].

**Decisions requested**
1. Commission a six-week review of option 3, reporting to you by [date].
2. Decide whether to renew the mass spectrometer contract in February on the current terms, on a short extension, or on terms matched to the review.
3. Agree an interim cost allocation for [period] that reflects usage, or confirm that the merger split stands.
4. Confirm how the technician role will be retained while the review runs.

I would welcome 30 minutes with you before Friday to go through the options.

oped-09__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

Tipping is unfair to the kitchen, but ending it without protecting servers' income is how you lose the people it's supposed to help. A small tip pool shared with the back of house is a better fix, and you can test it.

## The shape that clicked

```
unfair to the kitchen
  -> service charge tried: servers left
    -> tipping restored: kitchen still underpaid
      -> 4% pool: kitchen up, servers mostly whole
```

Your draft argued for and against ending tipping at the same time. The 2022 story and the 4% pool are the same lesson: the servers didn't reject paying the kitchen more, they rejected paying for it out of their own pockets without a say. Once the piece is organized around that, the two halves stop fighting.

## What moved

- **2022 story:** moved up to become the turn, because it shows why the obvious fix failed.
- **"Anyone should ask them first":** kept, and tied to your own admission that you didn't ask.
- **Tip pool:** moved to the end as the answer, with its limits stated.
- **Cut:** "The end I guess," and the repeated "I don't know" hedging. The uncertainty now lives in "one year at one restaurant."

## Rebuilt

**I Tried to End Tipping. The Servers Talked Me Out of It.**

Tipping in this country is broken, and everybody in the industry knows it. My line cooks make $17 to $19 an hour. On a good Friday my servers walk out with $350 or more in tips. Same shift, same heat, same chaos. The person plating your redfish makes a third of what the person carrying it makes. That isn't fair, and I've been trying to fix it for years.

So in 2022 we tried the fix that looked clean on paper: a 20 percent service charge and no tipping. Kitchen pay would go up, prices would be honest, and nobody would have to guess what to leave. Within two months we had lost three of our five servers. They could make more down the street, and some of them did.

One of them, Dee, had been with us since day one. She told me straight: "You're asking me to take a pay cut so you can feel good." She wasn't wrong. We went back to tipping after four months.

I think about that a lot. Servers in New Orleans are mostly women, many of them single moms, and tips are how they pay rent. Anyone who wants to abolish tipping should ask them first. I didn't, and it cost me.

But going back to the way things were isn't an answer either. The back of house is underpaid, and everybody knows it. Customers already balk at $45 entrées, so you can't fix the kitchen's wages by making the front of house take the hit.

What we did last year was smaller. We started a tip pool that sends 4 percent of tips to the kitchen. Louisiana allows a pool that includes back-of-house staff, as long as no managers take a share. Kitchen pay went up about $3.80 an hour. We lost one server, and he was leaving anyway.

That's one year at one restaurant, so I won't pretend it proves anything. But it points at what the service charge missed. The servers didn't object to the kitchen making more because they were greedy. They objected because the money was taken from them, without their say, to fix a problem they didn't create. A pool that moves a small slice of tips to the people cooking the food, decided with the staff, leaves most of the servers' income where it was and still closes part of the gap.

It won't close all of it. Four percent is a start. Owners who want to try this should talk to their servers before they touch the numbers, show them the math, and be willing to change the split if the front of house says it's too much. Ask the servers first. Dee would probably tell you the same.

## Check before you send

- **Louisiana rule:** confirm the tip-pool language is current. It's publishable, so get it right.
- **Dee:** ask whether she's okay being quoted by name.
- **Numbers:** confirm the $3.80 is an hourly average across all back-of-house staff, and that the 4% comes from total tips.
- **Missing:** if you have the actual dollar figure a server gives up per shift under the pool, add it. A concrete number will do more for skeptical readers than any line in the piece.

business-decision-03__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

Take the revenue-based financing, but only with a prepayment right and corrected repayment numbers. At any plausible Series A valuation, the angel's equity costs several times B's 1.4x, and the real risk is slipping past the 70k MRR gate, which neither offer fixes by itself.

## The shape that clicked

```
Gate:    35k MRR --(6-8%/mo)--> 70k MRR = Series A    ~month 9-12
Runway:  14 months with no new money
Raise:   start ~month 7-8 to close before month 14
         -> the squeeze is timing, not cost
A: $400k for ~6-7% equity  (~$400-500k of value at a $6-7M+ Series A)
B: $300k for $420k of revenue share  (~$120k nominal)
```

The two comparison tables come out even because they weigh cost of money against a gate the company must clear on time. Neither option is the thing that gets you to 70k MRR faster, unless the angel's SACCO access does.

## What moved

- **B's timeline:** 26-30 months becomes 38-44 months at 6-8% growth (1.07^n = 13). The payments are smaller early on, but the 1.4x takes about three years to collect.
- **Runway math:** $400k adds 8 months and $300k adds 5, which implies monthly burn near $50-60k, not $31k. Either fixed costs or hiring are missing from the burn figure, or the runway numbers are wrong.
- **Cut:** "Break-even at month 10-11" as a reason to borrow. If it holds, the cash buys buffer for the gate, not survival.
- **Missing:** what the money funds, whether $31k is gross or net, B's prepayment terms, and whether your Series A leads accept a revenue-share overhang.

## Rebuilt

**Decision:** Take the revenue-based financing, conditional on:

1. **A prepayment right** at a fixed multiple (for example 1.2x) once you close Series A or pass 70k MRR. This turns an open-ended 1.4x into a capped cost.
2. **A written payment schedule** at 6%, 8% and flat revenue, so the real duration is known before signing.
3. **Confirmation from your two Series A funds** that a revenue share ahead of their round is acceptable.

**Angel:** Decline the note as structured. Offer him an advisory role or a small option (roughly 0.25-0.5%) in exchange for named introductions to the SACCOs behind your three pipeline cooperatives. Judge him by whether those introductions close contracts within 90 days.

**When A wins instead:** if he commits in writing to specific introductions that bring in named cooperatives, his network may be worth more than 6-7% of the company. Without that commitment, the relationship is a benefit you cannot price, and the cost is.

business-decision-09__base.text:
**Recommendation: Start the Series A process now.** Launch within about 3 weeks, and treat the Q3 run and Cascadia's analysis as milestones you're racing toward during the process, not as prerequisites.

**Why:**

- **Waiting has a worse downside than starting.** If you wait for Q3 and the CM slips again, you'd start the process with about 7 months of runway. Fundraising takes 3 to 6 months, so you'd be negotiating from weakness with almost no buffer. Starting now gives you roughly 11 months of runway at launch, which leaves room to absorb a slip.
- **The margin story doesn't need to be realized to be compelling.** Investors fund trajectories all the time. A signed PO, a confirmed CM production schedule, and a unit-cost model you can defend will carry the argument. Showing up with 15,000 units already shipped is nice, but it isn't required.
- **Inbound interest decays.** Two firms asking about you is a real window. Waiting three to four months risks losing them to timing, not to your numbers.
- **Cascadia's analysis lands mid-process.** Its 6-week timeline fits inside a 3-to-4-month process. A 50,000-policyholder expansion, if it materializes, would be a strong late-stage catalyst.

**What would change my mind:** if the two inbound firms turn out to be tire-kickers, or if the CM can't commit to a Q3 schedule in writing within the next 2 to 3 weeks, the case for waiting gets stronger.

**Guardrail:** if you don't have a term sheet by about 7 months of runway (roughly $1.8M in the bank), activate the contingency plan: cut burn, pursue insider bridge options, and reassess.

---

**Revised pre-read section**

**Recommendation: Launch our Series A process in the next three weeks.**

**Position.** We have $3.1M in cash and burn of about $260k per month, or roughly 12 months of runway. We have shipped 4,200 Driplock units across two channels: about 3,300 through Cascadia Mutual's policyholder program and about 900 through direct online sales.

**Why now.**
1. *Downside protection.* Our Q3 run (15,000 units) has slipped twice before. If we wait for it and it slips again, we would start a raise with about 7 months of runway. Fundraising takes 3 to 6 months, so that scenario leaves almost no margin for error. Launching now gives us about 11 months of runway at kickoff and a buffer of several months to close.
2. *Inbound interest.* Our seed lead reports that two firms have asked about us. We'd rather engage them now than let the window close.
3. *Milestones arrive during the process.* Cascadia's actuarial analysis is due in about 6 weeks, and the Q3 run will be underway. We will present both as they land.

**What we'll show investors.**
- *Unit economics.* Current gross margin is 18% at $41 unit cost. The Q3 run is planned at 15,000 units and $23 unit cost, which we model at roughly 52% gross margin. [Insert CM confirmation/PO status here.]
- *Claims impact.* Cascadia's pilot data shows a 31% reduction in water-damage claims among households with a sensor. Cascadia has indicated interest in expanding to 50,000 policyholders if the analysis holds. We will share the full analysis when it's available.
- *Channel concentration.* About 79% of units come through a single insurer partner. We'll address how we're diversifying, including the direct channel's growth.

**Contingency.** If we do not have a signed term sheet by roughly 7 months of runway (about $1.8M cash), we will reduce burn, pursue insider bridge options, and bring a revised plan to the board.

**Board ask:** Approve the launch of the Series A process and the contingency trigger above.

---

Before you send this, verify three things: the CM's current written commitment on the Q3 schedule, whether the two inbound firms have shown real intent, and that the Cascadia figures are the pilot's own numbers rather than a preliminary estimate you'll need to caveat. If any of those come back weak, tell me and I'll adjust the recommendation.

pitch-04__skill_v1_1.text:
**The spine:** Polish housing cooperatives face rising heating costs and can't fund or wait out a typical custom retrofit. We install in 9 days with no facade work, and they pay from savings over 12-year contracts. The Łódź pilot shows it works.

Your deck is a feature tour. Each slide adds a fact, but none of them builds toward the question the investors already asked. Your pilot, the strongest evidence you have, sits at slide 7, after the competitor slide. Install speed and contract stickiness, which they asked about last time, are split across slides 4, 7, 8, and 9, so nothing ties them to the buyer's decision. The 27 LOIs also read as stronger than they are, since LOIs are usually non-binding.

```
Buyer's problem -> Why current options fail -> Proof (pilot) -> How it works
  -> Money (EaaS + grants) -> Why they stay -> Traction -> Who delivers -> Ask
```

**Proposed order**

1. **Title**
2. **The buyer's problem:** cooperative buildings on coal or old district heat, costs rising (merges 3 and 5)
3. **Why current options fail:** big brands focus on single-family homes, and large custom systems take 6-8 weeks with facade work (from 6)
4. **Pilot proof:** Łódź, 212 apartments, −41% per flat, 9-day installs (from 7, moved up)
5. **How it works:** modular cascade units in existing boiler rooms, no facade work (from 4)
6. **How the cooperative pays:** 12-year energy-as-a-service, grants covering 30-50% of capex (merges 8 and 10)
7. **Why they stay:** contract terms, who signs, renewal, switching cost (new slide, answers their stickiness question)
8. **Traction:** 27 signed LOIs, about 1,900 buildings, labeled honestly (from 9)
9. **Who delivers:** team, with Tomasz's crew tied to the install speed (from 2, moved to just before the ask)
10. **Ask:** €4M, use of funds, and Czech/Slovakia as a milestone, not a separate slide (merges 11 and 12)

**Cut or merge**
- Merge 8 and 10 into one financing slide.
- Fold the roadmap (11) into the ask. Czech and Slovak expansion before Polish proof reads as scope creep.
- Fold the competitor slide (6) into the problem and "why current options fail" slides. It's a contrast, not a standalone point.
- Keep the team slide, but move it later. Speed and proof land first, then the team explains who can deliver them.

**Missing, and likely to come up tomorrow**
- **Contract stickiness:** typical renewal rate, how long a board decision takes, whether members' assemblies must approve, and what a cooperative would lose by leaving. `[renewal terms]`, `[decision cycle]`
- **The 41% number:** what it's measured against, over what period, and whether weather was normalized. `[baseline and measurement period]`
- **Cooperative economics:** the monthly payment versus their old bill, and the payback period. `[monthly payment vs. prior bill]`
- **Install speed at scale:** how many crews you have and how many installs per month you can do. `[crew capacity]`
- **LOI status:** how many are binding, how many are in negotiation, and what conversion you expect. `[binding count]`

If you can fill in the stickiness and economics placeholders before tomorrow, slides 6 and 7 will do the most work in the meeting.

oped-01__base.text:
Starting with the permit increase and your own numbers pulls the reader in right away. The visitor grumbles can stay as a short aside.

---

Since April, a staff parking permit at Eastgate General costs £58 a month. It used to be £22. I know because I pay it, and because I've spent the months since working out what it means for the people I work with.

Take a band 5 nurse on nights. For many of them, the new charge comes close to a full shift's take-home pay every month. You are, in effect, paying to turn up for work.

For most of us there is no sensible alternative. Buses from my estate don't run before 6am or after 11pm. If you start at seven or finish after midnight, you drive. Nobody on nights is choosing a car park over a bus.

Of the nine nurses who left our ward this year, four mentioned parking in their exit interviews. Four out of nine is not a rounding error. Our ward manager told me the agency cover for those four posts has cost more than the Trust made from the permit increase across the whole hospital. I asked her to check it twice. She did.

Visitors have their own grumbles about the machines, the barriers and the overflow car park that floods every November, and I've shared most of them. This is a different problem. The Trust says the charges pay for maintenance and security, and I'm sure some of that is true. Car parks cost money. But the people paying this increase are the ones already doing the hardest shifts, and they're the ones we can least afford to lose.

I think the Trust should reverse the increase for night staff at the very least, and look again at whether anyone on a clinical rota should be paying this much to park at work. I'm not asking for a favour. I'm asking for the people who keep this place running to be able to get to it.

I love my job and I love this hospital. I just don't want to keep saying goodbye to colleagues over a car park.

---

**Before Friday, check these:**

- **The figures.** Confirm the £58/£22 and the April date against your payslip or the Trust's notice. Work out the take-home comparison on a real band 5 night rate, and keep the wording as "close to" unless the sum is exact.
- **Bus times.** Check the current timetables for your estate so the 6am and 11pm details are accurate.
- **The agency claim.** This is the most powerful line and the one a journalist will push on. Get the figures in writing from the ward manager or the Trust. If you can't, soften it to "I've been told" and say who told you.
- **Exit interviews.** Don't identify anyone, and check with your manager that using the numbers is fine.
- **Trust media policy.** Many NHS trusts ask staff to notify comms before speaking to the press, and some require sign-off. Check this now, because it could affect whether you can publish under your name.
- **The Trust's response.** The Gazette will probably ask for comment. Ask the Trust for a statement now so it can go in alongside your piece.

proposal-02__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

The charge is a funding mechanism for suburban buses. Emissions reduction is a side effect of the same drop in CBD entries, not a second goal of equal weight.

## The shape that clicked

```
 charge on CBD entry
        │
        ▼
 CBD entries fall ──────────► emissions fall (co-benefit)
        │
        ▼
 net revenue (the $310m)
        │
        ▼
 OSBU funded ──► 15-min buses in 14 corridors
        │
        ▼
 mode shift ──► fewer entries (loops back)
```

Your two stories are one loop, and the loop has a tension in it. Fewer entries means both more emissions savings and less revenue. Your memo currently treats these as additive, so the director sees two answers. Leading with the bus-funding story resolves it: the emissions gain is real, but the memo has to say what it costs in revenue.

## What moved

- **Bus funding:** moved to lead, because it is the only mechanism that makes the charge a commitment to a specific purpose, and it has the most specific evidence (38%, 14 corridors).
- **Emissions:** moved from co-equal to a consequence under the revenue point, with its trade-off stated.
- **Revenue volatility:** moved from a generic risk to a direct consequence of the loop above.
- **Cut:** nothing. The 40%-by-2032 scenario is kept but labelled as conditional on improved PT.
- **Missing:**
  - The entry-volume assumption behind the $310m.
  - Whether the 140kt and the 22-30% come from the same model.
  - A source for "consistent with international experience."
  - The 2032 modelling assumptions.

## Rebuilt

**Recommendation:** The Department should support a pilot cordon charge for the Melbourne CBD at $11 per weekday entry, from July 2026, with net revenue hypothecated to fund the Outer Suburban Bus Uplift (OSBU).

**Why this charge, and why it funds buses:**
- OSBU is currently unfunded beyond 2025-26.
- 38% of households in 14 growth-area corridors have no access to a 15-minute-frequency service. OSBU would extend frequent service to those corridors.
- The charge is estimated to raise $310m net a year [state the entry-volume assumption behind this figure]. That revenue would fund OSBU.

**Equity:** Lower-income outer-suburban residents are less likely to drive into the CBD (6% of trips from bottom-quintile postcodes), so the charge is mildly progressive, particularly when revenue funds OSBU.

**Emissions (a consequence of the same entry reduction):**
- Entries are expected to fall 22-30%, cutting cordon transport emissions by approx. 140kt CO2-e a year [confirm same scenario as the $310m].
- Modelling suggests entries could fall by up to 40% by 2032 if the charge is paired with improved public transport [state assumptions].
- Revenue falls as entries fall. The emissions gain and the revenue loss come from the same mechanism, and the memo should show both.

**Risks:**
- Revenue depends on entries falling, which is the intended outcome. Revenue volatility is therefore a design issue, not only a forecasting one.
- Business opposition from CBD retail.
- Tight legislative timeline.

team-01__skill_v1_1.text:

On 1 November, Platform stops being a separate team. Its 14 engineers join the four product domains so each one owns its own infrastructure, because waiting on a platform ticket went from 4 days to 11.

## The shape that clicked

```
Before
Product domains --> [Platform queue, 14 people] --> shared infra
                    avg wait: 11 working days

After (1 Nov)
Payments    --> owns payments infra
Lending     --> owns lending infra
Onboarding  --> owns onboarding infra
Risk        --> owns risk infra
DevEx (3, Joost) --> shared tooling and CI
```

Your draft tells the story in the order you lived it: wins, then surveys, then research, then the decision in paragraph four. The reader has to hold the question "what is changing?" for three paragraphs. The rewrite leads with the change, then the reason, then what it means for each group.

## What moved

- **Decision**: from paragraph 4 to the first paragraph, stated plainly.
- **Reason**: from scattered across three paragraphs to one block with the survey finding and the wait time together.
- **Ledger thanks**: from the opening to the close. It is still there, but it no longer delays the news.
- **"Nobody is losing their job"**: moved into a section for each group, so it answers the question each person is asking.
- **Cut**: "There's no perfect answer, but there were some clear patterns." It promises a pattern and never shows it. Replaced with a placeholder for the one reason you chose this option.
- **Kept, reframed: the 11 days.** It is your only hard evidence, so keep it. It reads as blame when it sounds like Platform's failure. In the rewrite it is the queue's number, and the sentence says the setup caused it. About 14 people reading this are Platform engineers, and they will read any Platform-specific stat as a verdict on them.
- **Check**: your draft says "11 working days" but "4 a year ago" without "working." Make both match.

## Missing

- `[Why this option over the alternatives you looked at]`
- `[What happens to open Platform tickets on 1 November]`
- `[Who people contact for shared-tooling questions, and how]`
- `[AMA time and link]`
- `[Confirm: who Platform engineers talk to this week about their domain]`

## Rebuilt

**Subject: Platform is joining the product domains from 1 November**

Team,

From 1 November, the Platform team stops existing as a separate group. Its 14 engineers join Payments, Lending, Onboarding and Risk, three or four per domain, and each domain owns its own infrastructure. Joost's Developer Experience group (3 people) stays as it is and keeps shared tooling and CI.
