A platform ticket now takes 11 working days on average, up from 4 a year ago. That's one queue serving four domains and 140 engineers, and it stopped working as we grew from 60. [Confirm this is your read.]

In Q3 I talked to leads across the org and looked at how similar companies have handled this stage. [One sentence: why this option over the others.]

What this means for you:

- **If you're on Platform:** your manager will talk to you individually this week about which domain you're joining. Nobody is losing their job.
- **If you're in a product domain:** you'll have 3 or 4 platform engineers from 1 November, and you'll own your infrastructure. [What happens to open platform tickets.]
- **Everyone:** shared tooling and CI questions still go to Developer Experience. [How to reach them.]

Managers will reach out individually this week. We'll run an AMA on Thursday at [time, link]. Bring the hard questions.

Thanks to everyone who carried the ledger migration. I'm proud of that work, and I know this is a lot to take in.

Marieke

team-04__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

The dashboard sells volume forecasts built on milk weights that are wrong at 40% of collection centres, so the collection fix is what makes Option A deliverable.

## The shape that clicked

```
Paper weights (40% of centres, ~9% error)
   -> wrong farmer payments -> support disputes up 60%
   -> farmer trust and supply erode
   -> volume data behind forecasts is unreliable
   -> dashboard (A) -> processor ARR (KES 14M, conditional)
```

The doc treats A and B as rival options. In this chain, B sits upstream of A's revenue, and the disputes are already eroding the supply the processors would buy.

## What moved

- **Option B:** from "ops priority" to prerequisite for A, since the dashboard reports volume by collection centre and those volumes come from the weights.
- **Processor ARR:** from headline revenue to probability-weighted, because all three deals are "will sign if," not signed.
- **Disputes:** from a morale risk under A to a churn and supply risk under the revenue case.
- **Cut:** "revenue matters most" as the only criterion. Runway is the real constraint, and both builds fit inside it.
- **Missing:**
  - Which collection centres fall in the supply areas of Kiambu Fresh, Rift Valley Creamery and the Nakuru processor.
  - Whether processors need live data or would accept a dashboard that labels data coverage.
  - Whether ops has a cheap interim fix for paper centres, such as photographing weigh slips.
  - A probability for each of the three deals.

## Rebuilt

**Decision:** Sequence the two builds rather than choose one.

**Recommendation:** Build offline-first collection entry (B) first, about 6 weeks. In parallel, sales runs processor pilots using centres that already have digital entry. Start the 8-week dashboard build when [trigger], for example when paper-centre error is below [target] or when a processor confirms in writing that a coverage-labelled forecast meets their needs. Total elapsed time is about 14 weeks, well inside the 11-month runway.

**Why:**
- Forecasts are only as good as the weights behind them.
- Payment disputes show the error already reaching farmers.
- B takes 6 weeks and addresses ops' core concern directly.
- A's deal risk is real, so the pilots reduce it instead of ignoring it.

**Risks and mitigations:**
- *Processor deals slip.* Pilot now and get written requirements from each processor.
- *Dashboard starts late.* Set the trigger date up front so it does not drift.

**When to put A first instead:** If most of the three processors' supply areas already use digital entry, the dashboard can ship on clean data and A-first becomes the better call.

Before you send this to Wanjiru, check the Missing items. Those answers could flip the recommendation.

oped-06__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

The phone ban is a good idea that was handed to teachers without the tools to enforce it, and the piece should ask for those tools.

## The shape that clicked

```
Ask: give teachers the tools the ban assumes
 ├─ Maddie (why it matters)         opens the piece
 ├─ Six colleagues (the gap)        the evidence
 └─ The classroom sound (what's at stake)   closes it
```

The old draft ended on "kids need to look up" without saying what the reader should do. Your husband's "so what do you want?" was the missing spine. Your strongest material, the colleagues' experience, is the case for that ask.

## What moved

- **Your ask**: moved from nowhere to the spine, because the piece needs a concrete request.
- **Colleagues' experience**: moved up from the middle to the centre, because it is the evidence for the ask.
- **Maddie**: kept as the opening, shortened, because she shows why the issue matters to families.
- **Classroom sound**: moved to the close, where it now points at what the ask protects.
- **"Mostly don't care"**: added a line answering it, so teachers are not made the villains.
- **Cut**: the "I cheered" line was shortened but kept, because it shows you support the ban.
- **Missing**: the specific ask. I have drawn the list from what your colleagues said they did not get. Please confirm or change it.

## Rebuilt

Last Thanksgiving my granddaughter Maddie, who is twelve, sat at our dinner table with her phone under the tablecloth. I don't think she meant to be rude. She's a lovely girl who plays hockey and still lets me braid her hair.

When I asked what she was watching, she couldn't really tell me. One video, then another. She said her friends do it in class too, and that teachers "mostly don't care."

I taught grades 7 and 8 in Peterborough for 31 years, and I don't think that's fair to teachers. Most of them care a great deal. What they've been handed is the problem.

When the province announced the classroom phone ban, I cheered, and I still think it was the right call. But I've since talked with six former colleagues who are still in the classroom. Not one has been given a locked pouch, a storage cabinet, or a single hour of training on how to enforce it. One told me she collects an average of eleven phones a day and loses the first ten minutes of every class to it. Another said her principal told staff to "use discretion," which she took to mean don't make waves with parents.

A ban that teachers must enforce alone is not really a ban. It's a wish.

So here is what I'm asking for. Give teachers the tools the ban assumes they have: [lockable pouches or storage in every classroom, training on enforcement, and one clear procedure from the board that replaces "discretion"]. These are modest requests, and they cost far less than the problem they solve.

My husband says I'm old-fashioned, and maybe I am. But I remember the sound of a classroom where everyone is thinking about the same thing at the same time. It's a sound you don't forget. I'd like Maddie's generation to hear it too, and I'd like their teachers to have what they need to bring it back.

Kids need to look up. Right now, the adults asked to help them do it are not being given the means.

strategy-01__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

We are losing accounts because they never get a team working in their first two weeks, so Q3 fixes early activation first and clears the SSO/SCIM deals that are blocking revenue, while the other items wait with stated reasons.

## The shape that clicked

```
Churn (118 accounts lost in H1)
 └─ Early activation fails
     ├─ No second teammate invited in 14 days (71% of churned vs 22% of retained)
     └─ No template setup in week one (retention 2.3x when completed)
         └─ No owner today  -> Q3 priority, with an owner
Blocked revenue: SSO/SCIM (4 deals, ~€210k ARR) -> Q3 priority, parallel track
Everything else -> sequenced, with a reason and a revisit point
```

The draft gave seven items equal weight, so it read as a list. Its strongest evidence sat in the middle, and onboarding was item seven, "time permitting." Putting the churn data at the center makes the other items answer one question: do they serve activation, or do they unblock revenue we already have? Deferred items with a reason and a revisit date read as sequencing, not refusal.

## What moved

- Retention data: from the middle of the draft to the opening, because it is the reason for everything else.
- Onboarding: from item seven "time permitting" to the first commitment, with an owner.
- SSO/SCIM: kept as the second commitment, because it is the only item tied to closed-in-hand revenue.
- Gantt redesign: deferred to Q4 with a reason, not dropped. Enterprise demand is real.
- Mobile, integrations, large boards, AI summary: sequenced behind the two commitments, each with a reason.
- Cut: none. Every item is in the document with a place.
- Missing: the 71% and 2.3x figures are associations, so the document says so and proposes tracking. You need a success metric, the squad split across the two commitments, and a decision from leadership on whether the Gantt work is locked to the upmarket plan.

## Rebuilt

**Q3 Core Workspace: Activation first**

Our churn problem starts in the first two weeks. Of the 118 accounts that churned in H1, 71% never invited a second teammate within 14 days, compared with 22% of retained accounts. Accounts that complete template setup in week one retain at 2.3 times the rate. These are associations, not proof that activation causes retention, so Q3 includes measuring whether improving activation moves retention.

Onboarding has no owner today. That changes this quarter.

**Q3 commitments**

1. **Activation (owner: [name]).** Improve second-teammate invites and week-one template setup for new accounts. Target: [X]% of new accounts invite a teammate within 14 days, up from [current]. Success is also measured by [retention metric, cohort].
2. **SSO/SCIM improvements.** Unblock the four deals currently waiting on this work, worth roughly €210k ARR combined. Allocation: [N] engineers.

Remaining engineering capacity ([N] engineers across two squads) goes to activation and to the SSO/SCIM work above.

**Deliberately not in Q3**

- **Gantt view redesign.** Enterprise customers have asked for this for over a year, and it supports the upmarket push. We are sequencing it after activation work and will revisit at Q4 planning [date]. [Decision needed: is this locked to the upmarket plan timeline?]
- **Mobile app refresh.** The 3.6 App Store rating is a real problem. [Option: scoped fix for rating recovery, if mobile can own it separately from the full refresh.]
- **Integrations marketplace (Jira, DATEV, Personio).** Strategic, and it will get capacity once activation metrics are on track.
- **Large-board performance (>5k tasks, ~40 accounts).** Affects a small, identifiable group; we will track it and schedule it for Q4.
- **AI summary feature.** Leadership interest is noted. We propose scoping it against a specific activation or retention use case before it takes engineering time.

academic-09__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

Most falls on this unit happened at night, when patients got up alone to use the bathroom, and the scripted toileting question at night rounds is the piece staff credit for the drop. Lead with that, and let Watson explain why asking about toileting is a caring act.

## The shape that clicked

```
BEFORE (procedural)              AFTER (relational, night-focused)
Falls -> risk -> tools           Night falls -> unassisted toileting
  (alarms, socks, education)       -> scripted question at 0200/0400
  Watson: background name-drop     -> Watson: the lens for why it works
  Purpose: vague "evaluate"        -> Purpose: test that link, with fidelity
```

The old draft led with theory and saved the finding for page 3. The finding is the most specific thing you have, so it should come first.

## What moved

- **Night-shift finding (para 5)**: moved from the end of the draft to the problem statement, because it defines the problem.
- **Watson (para 1)**: moved from the opening to the framework section, where it does analytic work on the toileting finding instead of sitting as background.
- **Bundle details (para 4)**: moved into the project description, after the problem is established.
- **Generic strategy list (para 3)**: shortened. Its job is now to show the gap.
- **Purpose (para 6)**: made specific. It now names the unit, the framework, and what is being examined.
- **Cut**: "Interestingly," and "significant concern," which told the reader nothing.

Missing:
- **Citations** for the national rate (3–5 per 1,000 patient days), the sentinel event statement, and Watson's primary text.
- **Background sentence** on why the reviews found mixed evidence, if you can cite one.
- **Denominator check**: 23 + 9 = 32 falls at baseline and 6 + 7 = 13 after, but the rates are 4.1 and 1.6 per 1,000 patient days. Confirm both periods use the same patient-day counts and state the baseline period, because your chair will check.
- **Fidelity data**: the purpose needs a measure of how well rounding was done (for example, the percent of scripted questions asked), if you have it.
- **Causal caveat**: the staff attribution is an interview finding about a multi-component bundle, so the draft says "associated with" and "staff identified."

## Rebuilt

**Problem statement**

Falls remain a persistent harm in acute care. National data place rates at 3–5 per 1,000 patient days, and falls can cause injury, extend length of stay, and add cost [citation]. The Joint Commission classifies patient falls as a sentinel event [citation]. On our 32-bed medical-surgical unit, falls were not spread evenly across the day. In the baseline period, 23 of 32 falls occurred at night, and most of those involved patients getting up alone to use the bathroom. The problem was not only that falls happened, but when and why they happened.

**Background**

Fall prevention strategies include bed alarms, hourly rounding, yellow socks, and patient education. Evidence for these approaches is mixed (Ortega, 2016; Bianchi & Hale, 2019). [Add one sentence on why the reviews found this variation, if a source supports it.] Most of these strategies respond to fall risk in general. Few are designed around the specific moments when patients are most likely to move without help.

**Project description**

From January to June 2024, our unit implemented a fall prevention bundle with three components: purposeful hourly rounding that included a scripted toileting question, bedside shift report that included fall risk, and a "call, don't fall" whiteboard. Falls decreased from 4.1 to 1.6 per 1,000 patient days. Most of the reduction occurred on night shift, where falls fell from 23 to 6, while day falls changed from 9 to 7. Staff interviews suggested that the scripted toileting question at the 0200 and 0400 rounds was the key component.

**Theoretical framework**

Watson's Theory of Human Caring places the nurse–patient relationship at the center of healing and frames safety as relational rather than merely procedural [citation]. Within this framework, the scripted toileting question is a caring act: it anticipates a need the patient may not raise before getting up alone. The project uses this lens to examine whether a relational practice at a predictable point of need is associated with fewer falls, a question that equipment and reminders alone do not address.

**Purpose**

This DNP project evaluates the implementation of a fall prevention bundle on a 32-bed medical-surgical unit, guided by Watson's Theory of Human Caring. The project asks how the bundle was implemented, including [fidelity measure, if available], and whether changes in fall rates, particularly on night shift, follow implementation.

positioning-03__base.text:
The numbers suggest your instinct is right about where the business is, but Ciarán's instinct about the sports work isn't wrong either. The trouble is that the current page tries to serve both without choosing a lead.

**What the data says**

- Over-60s are 58% of new patients and generate far more care. Per 100 new patients, that's roughly 557 sessions from over-60s versus about 111 from sports patients (ignoring the 15% in other categories). Sports patients are valuable, but they're a shorter relationship.
- The 22-person waitlist means demand for your older-adult offering already exceeds capacity. Your homepage isn't what's holding that segment back.
- Sports patients arrive through Instagram and the GAA club, which are different channels from the GP and word-of-mouth flow that brings older patients. Different channels often need different landing pages.
- The reviews match the segments. Older patients praise patience, explanation, and access. Sports patients praise outcomes. Both are strong testimonials.

**Three options**

**1. One page, leading with recovery and older adults**
Opening: *"Get moving again, and keep moving. Physiotherapy in Rathmines for hips, knees, balance and everyday strength, with the time to explain what's going on and a plan you understand."*
- Pros: matches your revenue, waitlist, and referral sources. Your best reviews are already about this.
- Cons: Ciarán's sports work gets buried, and Instagram traffic may bounce.

**2. One page, leading with performance**
Opening: *"Get back to your sport, stronger. Performance physiotherapy in Rathmines for ACL rehab, running gait analysis and return to play."*
- Pros: clear, energetic, and matches Ciarán's expertise and the "premium" feel he wants.
- Cons: it targets the segment that averages 4.1 sessions and doesn't fill the waitlist. You'd be marketing toward your smaller revenue stream while your larger one is referral-driven and already working.

**3. One homepage with two clear doors, plus dedicated sub-pages (my recommendation)**
Hero: *"Physiotherapy in Rathmines that gets you back to what matters to you."*
Two cards beneath:
- *"Sport and training"*: ACL rehab, gait analysis, return to play. Link to a sports page that can be the destination for Instagram and GAA campaigns.
- *"Recovery and staying independent"*: hip and knee replacement recovery, falls prevention, strength and balance. Link to a page that carries the waitlist and the "explained everything" story.

This keeps the homepage honest about being a two-part clinic without the mushy "for every body" copy. It also gives each partner a proper home for their work and lets you test which door converts better.

**Option 4, if you want a cheaper version:** keep the current structure but build two campaign landing pages, one for Instagram/GAA and one for GP referral materials. This often gets most of the benefit of two sites.

**Things to settle before March**

- Replace the stock images with real photos of your team and the clinic, one set per segment. A rugby photo and a garden photo tell visitors the page is generic.
- Stop using "every body" and similar claims. Use specific language from your reviews instead.
- Check sports margin per session. If performance work is priced higher or runs with better margins, Ciarán's "premium" argument has real financial backing, and it should shape how you present that segment.
- Decide what you want to be known for in three years. That's a more useful question than which partner is right.

If you tell me more about pricing by segment or how the GAA relationship works, I can help draft the two sub-page intros as well.

team-05__base.text:
Your instinct is right. The paper asserts a conclusion that its own evidence doesn't yet support, and a trustee with HR experience will find that gap quickly.

**1. The headline doesn't match the evidence.** The paper says "the core issue is pay," but in your own account pay was raised directly by one of four leavers. Three of four mentioned isolation, two called holiday clubs the "final straw," and the caseload rise was from about 25 to 45 volunteers per coordinator, roughly 80%. That is a bigger structural change than a £3,100 salary gap. You may still conclude pay matters, but you need to show why, not assert it. As written, the paper reads as though the evidence was selected to fit a conclusion.

**2. The pay proposal doesn't close the gap it cites.** The departing coordinator was offered £27,000. Your proposal is £26,500, so even your own benchmark is £500 above what you're offering. Someone will ask whether this would have kept her.

**3. The cost figure is wrong or unclear.** £3,100 × 7 posts = £21,700, which is the salary uplift alone, not the figure "including on-costs." Employer NI and pension will add meaningfully to that. Also clarify whether the figure assumes seven filled posts or whether the four vacancies are costed in. Get the fully loaded number right before Thursday.

**4. "Below comparable roles in the sector" has no source.** Name the benchmark: a sector pay survey, comparable local posts at councils or housing associations, or the job adverts you looked at. Without this, the claim is an assertion.

**5. The recommendation is a single lever with no alternatives.** Trustees will ask what else was considered and what each option would cost. At minimum, compare:
- Pay uplift only
- Caseload reduction (e.g. a cap of 30, or a second coordinator per area)
- Reinstating peer supervision (possibly cheap or free)
- Changing holiday club rota or making it voluntary
- A combined package, possibly staged

Some of the non-pay fixes may be cheaper and address more of what leavers said.

**6. Sustainability is missing.** A permanent salary increase is recurring cost, but you're proposing to fund it from a one-off designated reserve. Trustees will ask what happens in year two. Show the multi-year cost and where it comes from.

**7. The cost of inaction isn't stated.** Quantify it: recruitment and onboarding costs for four posts, lost volunteer capacity across 180 volunteers, the Reading Buddies pause and its effect on schools, and the reputational and funder implications.

**8. "We will continue to monitor" is not a plan.** Set out what you'll measure, over what period, and what would count as success, e.g. coordinator turnover at six or twelve months, volunteer retention, and supervision attendance. Commit to reporting back.

**9. Add a "what we don't know" section.** Four exit interviews is a small sample. Say so. Trustees generally respect honesty about limits more than confident claims that can be picked apart.

**A stronger structure might be:**
1. What happened (numbers, impact on volunteers and schools)
2. What leavers told us, in a simple table: four leavers × reasons cited, anonymised
3. Options considered, with costs and expected effect
4. Recommendation: possibly a staged package, e.g. address caseload and supervision now, adjust pay to a benchmarked level, and review at six months
5. Risks, funding source, and measures of success
6. The decision you're asking trustees to take

If you can share the exit notes (anonymised), the sector pay data you have, and the current caseload and holiday-club rota, I can help you draft the options table and cost comparison. That would make the paper much harder to pick holes in, and it would give your CEO a stronger case to take to the board.

pitch-06__base.text:
Restructure around the CISO's problem, not your company. Your current deck opens with you and ends with the problem. Flip that: open with the risk they carry, use the case as the proof, and move the company facts to the end.

**New order (~25 min, leave 10 for discussion)**

1. **Opening question:** "How would you know today if someone on your team was quietly moving money out?" One line, no logo-heavy title slide.
2. **Why current controls miss this:** Threshold rules and per-transaction alerts only see single events. Insider fraud is built from many small ones that each look normal.
3. **What it looks like over time:** Anonymized case study as a timeline: "a back-office analyst, dormant accounts, small beneficiary changes, R$ 2.3M moved before detection." Describe the pattern, not the bank. Let the CISO make the connection himself.
4. **What the exposure is:** Estimate the R$ 11M+ counterfactual, and be ready to explain how you calculated it, because the analyst will ask.
5. **What good looks like for them:** Detection before loss, low false-positive load on the SOC, LGPD-compliant from day one, no rip-and-replace.
6. **How it works, in their terms:** Your architecture slide, simplified to three boxes: their data sources → per-employee behavioural baselines → alerts that drift from baseline. Lead with the systems they already own.
7. **What their analyst sees:** A screenshot or short demo of a case timeline with risk score drift. This is the slide that wins over the analyst. Make it concrete.
8. **Privacy and governance by design:** LGPD masking, role-based access, who can see what, and how HR and legal stay in the loop. Address this before anyone asks.
9. **Fits your stack:** Cut the 40+ logos to the 5–8 systems a bank this size likely runs (core banking, AD, email gateway, SIEM). Ask them to confirm which apply.
10. **Deployment plan:** 6–8 weeks, week by week, with what their team has to provide in each phase.
11. **Proposed pilot:** Scoped to one data source (e.g., beneficiary-change logs on dormant accounts), with agreed success metrics and an exit point.
12. **Pricing options:** Tie tiers to pilot scope and rollout, not a feature grid.
13. **Who we are:** One slide. Founded 2019, 60 people, SP and Lisbon, ISO 27001, investors and awards. Keep it short and late.
14. **Q&A / next steps**

**Practical tips**

- **Don't mention the public incident.** Structuring the case around the pattern lets the CISO make the link, which is more respectful and more persuasive.
- **Prepare for the analyst.** Expect questions on false-positive rates, how baselines handle people who legitimately change roles, how the R$ 11M figure was estimated, and data retention under LGPD. Have answers ready, or say you'll follow up in writing.
- **Consider presenting in Portuguese** if the analyst's English is uncertain. Technical depth lands better that way.
- **Leave the pilot on the screen** when Q&A starts. It's your close.

If you paste your architecture and case-study text, I can draft the one-line slide headlines in full.

business-decision-01__skill_v1_1.text:
Your notes already contain the answer, and it's not oven versus hire. The oven would fix the baguette shortfall, but it wouldn't fix the 4am problem, and you're the 4am problem.

**What you're missing**

1. **The oven doesn't reduce your hours. It makes the 4am shift more productive, and you still work it.** You'd be buying more capacity for a shift only you can run. You'd also have an €18k machine that needs someone trained on it, and Margaux may leave before that's sorted.

2. **The bank saying yes to the oven is not evidence the oven is the right call.** Lenders will finance equipment because it has resale value. They won't finance a salary, but the salary is the thing that gives you time off. Of the two options, the one the bank approves is the one that doesn't address your constraint.

3. **The second baker has to pay for itself, and at your margins it might not.** Your net margin is around 9% on €31k, roughly €2,800 a month. A €2,600–2,900 hire would absorb almost all of that unless it brings in new profit. Your lost sales are maybe €3.9k–5.2k a month if you trade about 26 days (my arithmetic from your rough €150–200/day). Whether that's worth hiring for depends on your gross margin on bread, which you didn't mention and which matters more than anything else in this decision.

4. **Margaux's "might move next year" is the deadline that matters.** If she leaves, you'll need a baker regardless. Better to plan that replacement now, while she can train them, than in a panic.

**What I'd do**

Don't commit to either. Spend the next three weeks on two things:

- **Measure the demand.** For two weeks, record the exact time you sell out and how many people ask for something you've run out of. That tells you whether the lost €150–200/day is real and whether it's baguettes or your whole range.
- **Find out your gross margin per baguette and per pastry.** Without it, you can't tell whether extra sales pay for a salary.

Then, if the numbers hold, the order I'd lean toward is **hire first, oven second**. A junior baker covering the 4am shift gets you sleep and days off, lets you train toward Margaux's replacement, and makes the oven a later, better-informed decision. You can also ask the oven supplier whether the 10-week lead time allows a deposit with a later delivery date, so you aren't locked in.

Your accountant is looking at the spreadsheet, and your mum is looking at you. You haven't had two days off in a row since 2022. That's the number I'd weight most heavily.

Two questions that would sharpen this: what's your gross margin on baguettes, and do you sell out of other products before 11h, or only tradition?

oped-05__skill_v1_1.text:
## The spine

Sorghum paid more than maize for two seasons, but only because one buyer promised a fixed price. The real question for 2025 is what happens to that promise, and that should be the post.

## The shape that clicked

```
SORGHUM income
├─ price: KSh 3,300 (contract)      ← the hinge
└─ volume: 100% of harvest → 60% (2025 review)

MAIZE income
├─ good season: 9 bags × 2,800 (2022)
└─ dry season: 4 bags × 4,100, little to sell (2023)
```

Both openings argue from the same numbers and both skip the hinge. Your wife's point is that each one tells a single season's story. Neither mentions the 60% clause, which changes the sorghum math more than the price does.

Gross income per acre, before costs:

- Sorghum on full contract: 7 bags = KSh 23,100; 8 bags = KSh 26,400
- Sorghum if capped at 60% (rest sold at KSh 2,200): 7 bags ≈ 20,000; 8 bags ≈ 22,900
- Maize, average of your two seasons: about KSh 20,800

With the cap, sorghum and maize are roughly even on revenue. The decision then depends on costs and risk, which you haven't given me. This assumes the uncapped 40% sells at the open-market price.

## What moved

- **60% volume cap:** missing from both openings, now the spine.
- **2023 maize shortfall:** your strongest case against maize, but it is one dry season. Keep it, labelled as one season.
- **Quelea losses (about 1 bag/acre):** a real cost of sorghum that neither opening mentions. Move it into the sorghum section.
- **Kiprono's 2024 result:** hearsay, so cut it unless you get his numbers.
- **Missing:** per-acre costs for each crop (seed, fertiliser, labour, transport, spraying); whether your 7 and 8 bag figures are before or after quelea; Kiprono's 2024 bags and price; any 2025 terms in writing; the date of the price review.

## Rebuilt

**Working title:** What sorghum paid me, and what happens when the buyer changes the deal

**Opening (full):**
Two seasons of sorghum on a fixed contract paid me better than maize ever did on my six acres. Then Kerio Valley Malt wrote to say it will review the price in 2025 and may take only 60% of what I grow. I have spent the last month working out what that means, and it is not the answer I would have given a year ago.

**Outline:**
1. **The numbers.** Per-acre table of maize (2022, 2023) and sorghum (2023, 2024), gross, with the one-season caveat stated plainly.
2. **What the cap does.** The 60% calculation above, with the assumption about the remaining 40% stated.
3. **What the cap doesn't show.** Quelea losses and [your per-acre costs for each crop].
4. **What I'm doing for 2025.** [Your plan, e.g. planting split between crops, or asking the buyer for written terms.]
5. **Close.** The rule you would give a neighbour in your position, in one or two sentences.

**Which to write:** Option A's arc is the stronger draft, but only once the 60% cap is in it. Option B's uncertainty is the honest part, so it belongs in the closing section rather than as the opening. Write the post once you have the 2025 terms and Kiprono's numbers, or write it now and say plainly that the price review hasn't happened yet. Either way, the cap should be in the first three paragraphs.

talk-04__base.text:
You're right to feel uneasy. The verification finding is bigger than either feature, and it undercuts the recommendation. Bill splitting is pitched as a viral growth driver through invites, but 61% of Q2 signups never verified and so never transacted. Invites from people who can't send money won't go far. And if invitees also need to verify, the selfie-match failure rate becomes a bottleneck for the viral loop itself.

Don't frame this as "the question is wrong." Answer A or B directly, then say what has to be true for that answer to hold. Something like: "If we're choosing between these two features, bill splitting edges out savings goals. But neither matters much until we fix activation, which is losing most of our new users before they transact. I'd fix that first."

Here's a rewrite:

---

**Recommendation**
1. **Fix identity verification first (this sprint).** 61% of Q2 signups never verified, and the selfie-match step fails on first attempt 44% of the time. Users who fail once verify at under half the rate of those who pass. This is the largest lever we can see, and the fix is likely cheaper than building a feature.
2. **Then build bill splitting** over savings goals. It has a slightly higher survey preference (34% vs 29%), and it's the stronger fit for invite-driven growth, provided new users can actually transact.

**Why not savings goals?** Stated demand is lower, and both features exist in Kova and Tuppence, so neither gives us an obvious edge. Several users keep a second app for one of these functions, which suggests we could take that share with either.

**Findings**

*Feature demand (survey, n=1,180):* Bill splitting 34%, savings goals 29%. The gap is modest, and survey requests are stated preference, so treat it as a tiebreaker rather than a strong signal.

*Age pattern (interviews, n=24):* Users 21–27 leaned toward bill splitting; users over 30 leaned toward savings goals. This is directional only, given the sample size.

*Activation (funnel + interviews):*
- 61% of Q2 signups never completed ID verification and never transacted.
- Selfie-match fails on first attempt 44% of the time, and the main drop-off is at this step.
- 9 of 24 interviewees nearly gave up during ID upload.
- 3 of 24 finished only because a friend had sent them money and they needed to verify to withdraw it. Money in transit seems to be a strong completion trigger, which may matter for bill splitting too.

**Open questions before committing**
- Do invitees need to verify before they can split a bill with someone? If so, verification is a dependency for the viral loop.
- What does a selfie-match fix cost, and how confident are we it moves first-attempt pass rates?

---

Before Friday, I'd check three things:

1. **Does bill splitting require verified invitees?** This is the most important factual question. If yes, your case for bill splitting depends on the verification fix, which strengthens the sequencing argument.
2. **Is the 5-point survey gap meaningful?** With n=1,180 it's probably real, but check how the question was worded and whether it was asked of everyone or only certain segments.
3. **Get an estimate for the selfie-match fix.** Execs will ask what it costs and what it's worth. Even a rough range (e.g., "if we recover a third of the 44% first-attempt failures, that's X more verified users per month") makes the case concrete.

Presenting it this way answers their question, shows you've thought about what sits beneath it, and gives them a decision they can act on Friday. Leading with the verification problem is not a dodge, provided you still give them the A/B answer.

proposal-09__base.text:
Your instinct to avoid overselling is right, and that same discipline is what will make the memo persuasive. Right now it's defensive for three reasons: it hedges the main result, it leans on the strike and turnover without quantifying them, and it presents the 17-point finding in a way that invites the board to treat it as proof. A board that is already skeptical will read that combination as special pleading.

The stronger move is to say plainly that the original model didn't work as designed, then argue for a different, testable investment. That is a more credible renewal case, not a weaker one.

**What to change**

- **Lead with the miss.** State the 4-point result and that it wasn't significant, in the first paragraph. Boards trust officers who name bad news first.
- **Separate the original theory from the new hypothesis.** The evidence doesn't show the training model raised reading scores in this setting. It does suggest that a coaching model may work, but that is a new hypothesis, and it should be labeled as one. Calling it a "refinement" that rescues the original theory will look like moving goalposts.
- **Treat the 11-school result as a signal, not a finding.** The schools volunteered, so they may differ systematically (more motivated principals, stronger teachers, better baselines). The lower turnover could be a selection effect too. Say this yourself. It's the single most effective credibility move available to you.
- **Make the renewal conditional and testable.** Instead of renewing for all 40 schools on the current model, fund the coaching model with a design that can actually answer the question.
- **Quantify the disruptions or drop them as explanations.** "The strike and turnover explain it" is unfalsifiable without numbers. If you can't show how much of the gap they account for, present them as context, not as the reason.
- **Use the co-funding offer carefully.** The secretariat's interest and 40% cost-share is a real and useful signal of institutional demand and sustainability. It is not evidence of effect. Present it as a sustainability argument.

**Possible structure**

1. **Decision requested:** Renew for R$2.6M over three years, restructured around a coaching-model test with defined gates. Not a continuation of the current model across all 40 schools.
2. **What happened:** The original model produced a 4-point gain, not significant against comparison schools. Strike and turnover were real headwinds; we are not yet able to say how much they explain.
3. **What we learned:** In 11 volunteer schools piloting fortnightly coaching, gains averaged 17 points. Selection bias is a serious concern, and we cannot attribute this to coaching yet.
4. **Proposed design:** Year 1 expands coaching to a larger set of schools, with assignment to coaching or comparison done by lottery among eligible schools, and an independent evaluator with pre-agreed outcomes. Funding for later years is released only if interim implementation and early outcome benchmarks are met. (Set specific thresholds with Rede Aprender and the evaluator before the board meeting.)
5. **Risks:** Selection in the pilot, turnover, dependence on the municipality's co-funding, and the possibility that the effect doesn't hold at scale.
6. **Why still fund:** Strong financial controls, clean audit, a credible partner in the secretariat, and a model that is cheap to test relative to the cost of scaling a failed one.

**On the board members**

Go to them before the meeting. Tell them what you told me: the original result missed, you're not defending it, and you're recommending a different, falsifiable bet with a built-in exit. Ask what evidence would change their minds. If the answer is "nothing," you've learned something about the decision; if it's specific, you can design toward it.

If you share the evaluation data (baselines, comparison-group details, turnover by school), I can help you check whether the 11-school pattern survives any reasonable adjustment, and draft the gate criteria. That analysis would also tell you how much weight the coaching finding can bear before the board sees it.

talk-09__base.text:
Pick the onboarding story, but not as a compromise between Jens and Aylin. The data doesn't support either of their claims.

**Headline:** Q3 churn is concentrated in customers acquired through the MedPraxis reseller channel, who were never successfully set up. Price and support delays are not the main driver.

**Why it's not price:** Customers older than 12 months got the same 12% increase and churned at 1.4%, which is normal. If price were the driver, the tenured base should show it too.

**Why it's not support:** Same logic. Tenured customers lived through the same doubled response times without churning. Support delays may matter for new customers who need help during setup, but that makes them an amplifier, not the cause.

**Why it's onboarding:**
- 55 of 94 churned accounts (59%) came through the reseller channel.
- 16 of 38 exit survey responses (42%) say they didn't use it enough or never got set up properly, the top reason by a wide margin. Price got 9 and support got 7.
- The reseller does onboarding and you can't see their notes or checklists. That's a visibility gap, and it's where the failure most likely sits.

**Gaps to close before Monday:**
1. **Reseller cohort size.** You need the total number of reseller-acquired customers, not just the churned ones. If 55 churned out of, say, 300, that's an ~18% churn rate, which is a much stronger story than "59% of churn." Get this number first.
2. **Pricing for the reseller cohort.** Check whether their intro or promo pricing expired around 1 July. If so, price could be an amplifier for this group, and Jens gets a partial win without it being the root cause. Tell leadership this before Jens raises it.
3. **Ticket data for churned accounts.** Did they file support tickets, and were those tickets setup-related? If yes, Aylin's point holds for onboarding capacity, just not as the churn cause.
4. **Activation metric.** Time to first booking or first scheduled appointment, by channel. This directly tests the onboarding story.
5. **Partner conversation.** Ask MedPraxis for onboarding completion rates and call notes for the 55 accounts. Even a few calls with churned customers would strengthen the case a lot.

**How to handle Jens and Aylin:**
- For Jens: "Price didn't drive this. Tenured customers absorbed the same increase at normal churn. The problem is concentrated in one acquisition channel, which is a go-to-market question, and Sales owns the partner relationship." That's a real ownership conversation, so give him a role in the fix. Don't frame it as clearing his team.
- For Aylin: "Support response times did degrade, and it likely hurt new customers during setup. But the churn is concentrated in customers who never got activated, so headcount alone won't fix it. If onboarding support capacity is the gap, we should make that case specifically, with ticket data." That keeps her headcount case alive if the data supports it.

**Suggested Monday slide headline:** "Q3 churn is concentrated in under-activated reseller customers. Price and support delays are contributing factors but don't explain the pattern."

That replaces "multiple factors contributed" with a specific claim, names the factors you ruled in or out, and shows what you'll do next. Leadership will respond better to that than to a pick that falls apart under questions.

If you can share the reseller cohort size and whether their pricing changed on 1 July, I can help you tighten the numbers and draft the talk track.

**Recommend B, but pair it with a line that tells donors what their money does.**

**Why neither tagline fixes the problem:** Both are about the tenant or about a value. Neither tells a donor what they'd be buying. "Everyone deserves a safe home" is a sentiment almost any housing charity could claim. "Know your rights. Keep your home." is more concrete, and "keep your home" connects to your strongest result, but it speaks to the person in crisis. Your donors are mostly homeowners over 50, so the page needs to show them their role and the impact.

Your page already has the strongest material, and it's all in the board's report, not on the page: 6,840 calls, $35 per call, and the 64% tenancy-retention figure. The current ask ("Donate today to support our work") gives the donor nothing concrete to respond to.

**Suggested donate-page copy:**

> **Know your rights. Keep your home.**
> Your $35 covers one full call to a tenant facing eviction, including follow-up. In 2023, we answered 6,840 calls from renters across Toronto.
>
> [Give $35 — fund one call] [Give $50] [Give $100] [Other]

Keep the body copy you have; it's good. Put the impact line directly under the tagline.

**On the 64% figure, be careful:** Callers who used prep sessions probably differ from unrepresented tenants generally. They may be more motivated or further along in the process. Your partner clinic's ~40% is an estimate of a different population. Don't present 64% vs 40% as "we improve outcomes by 24 points." Say something like: "Of callers who had a hearing scheduled and used our prep sessions in 2023, 64% kept their tenancy." That's accurate and still persuasive.

**For the five minutes:**

1. Recommend B as the tagline, since it's the only option that names a specific result.
2. Propose adding the $35/call line and the 2023 call count to the donate page, since the numbers the board values are currently invisible to donors.
3. Flag that online giving fell from $14,900 to $11,200. A tagline won't reverse that alone. The ask and the donor's role matter more. Mailing or print appeals to your 50+ homeowner base may matter as much as the web page.

## The spine

Margin management and agrochemical exposure act on the same wild bees in the same places, and the question is whether they compound or buffer each other.

## The shape that clicked

```

          |                                  |
          v                                  v
   Nest density & forage          Residues in pollen loads
          \                                  /
           v                                v
        Wild bee persistence in the 18 shared sites
                          ^
                          |
        Volunteer bumblebee records, same districts (WP3)
```

Right now the three WPs sit side by side because each answers a different question at a different place. The 18 shared sites are already the spine. Once the design is built around them, WP1 and WP2 measure both sides of one interaction, and WP3 becomes a way to test whether the result holds beyond one genus.

## What moved

- **WP1 and WP2**: merged into one exposure-by-management design at the shared sites, because they now answer one question.
- **WP3**: demoted from a standalone package to a monitoring instrument for the same margins and districts. If it cannot be tied to those sites, cut it and say so.

## Rebuilt

**Central question:** Does the mowing regime of field margins buffer or compound wild bees' exposure to agrochemicals in intensively farmed landscapes?

**Aims**
1. Quantify how margin mowing frequency affects ground-nesting bee density (WP1), at 40 margins with [N] paired sites.
2. Quantify neonicotinoid and fungicide residues in *Osmia bicornis* pollen at the same sites, and test whether residue load differs by margin regime (WP2).
3. Test whether the pattern holds for bumblebees, using a validated volunteer monitoring tool in the same districts (WP3; validation target [X]% across [N] species).

**Opening paragraph (draft):** Field margins are meant to support pollinators, but their management may change how much agrochemical exposure bees receive. We test this in Lower Saxony, where a 2023 pilot found nest density 2.3 times higher in margins mown once rather than three times a year, and where 68% of pollen samples from *Osmia bicornis* contained residues, most often fungicide mixtures. [Explain why the paired design answers the question.]

**Before you submit, check:**
- Residues in pollen reflect forage from the surrounding landscape, not just the margin. Say how you will separate margin effects from neighbouring-field effects, or list it as a limitation.
- Several volunteers are farmers or neighbours of the sites. Declare this, obtain consent, and consider a verified subset of records and blind residue analysis to show that management regime did not influence results.

## The spine

Don't put "should we do this deal" to a vote. The 50/50 split comes from packaging several separable decisions into one yes/no, and the one that decides the question is exclusivity. Ask the team to agree on the conditions under which Nadi signs.

## The shape that clicked

```
Deal (one vote)                     Reframed
├─ Revenue   ─────────────┐         Exclusivity  → negotiate. Only term
├─ Brand (white-label)    ├─ mixed     that blocks the ~40-hospital
├─ Exclusivity (4 yrs)  ──┘              pipeline (Medisetu, Kaveri)
└─ ECG AI delay (5 mo)               White-label → acceptable if Arogya
                                        runs onboarding (the adherence driver)
                                     ECG AI delay → price it, then gate on it
```

Pros and cons mix the items together, so they cancel out and each camp can quote a different one. Pulled apart, the debate is mostly about one term.

## What moved

- **Exclusivity**: from one bullet among the pros and cons → the decision itself. It is the only term that forecloses options you don't yet have.
- **Pilot adherence (84% vs 61%)**: from a point in favor of revenue → evidence for why hospital onboarding matters. It is a two-hospital pilot, so treat it as directional.
- **ECG AI delay**: from a con → a cost to price before the vote.
- **Investor sentiment**: kept, but it doesn't bear on exclusivity, so it doesn't decide the question.
- **Missing**: value of the Medisetu and Kaveri pipeline (probability and deal size), cost of the five-month delay, what "protect the brand" would concretely lose, and whether "probably negotiable" is confirmed in writing.

## Rebuilt: 15-minute slot

**0–2 min: Reframe.** "Both camps agree the risk is exclusivity. Today we decide the conditions for signing, not whether to sign."

**2–5 min: Facts nobody disputes.**
- ₹1.8 Cr upfront, plus ₹420 per patient per month. At Arogya's projected 3,000 patients for a full 12 months, that's about ₹1.5 Cr a year. It's a ceiling, since patients ramp up through the year.
- Exclusivity covers Karnataka and Telangana for four years, which is where Medisetu and Kaveri Care sit (about 40 hospitals combined).
- Pilot adherence: 84% with hospital onboarding, 61% direct, from two hospitals.

**5–8 min: Price what's unpriced.** Pipeline value: [probability × deal size]. Delay cost: [what the ECG AI slip costs in revenue or position]. Brand: [what a white-label patient-facing absence actually costs us, if anything].

**8–12 min: Vote on the rule, not the deal.** Three options:
- **A.** Sign only if exclusivity is removed, or narrowed to Arogya's own facilities or a time limit, or carved out for named pipeline chains.
- **B.** Sign as drafted.
- **C.** Decline.

Pick one. If A wins, agree on the walk-away point.

**12–15 min: Owners and next step.** One person confirms in writing whether exclusivity is negotiable and returns with Arogya's answer. Another prices the ECG AI delay. The CEO gets a decision: a counter-offer with a walk-away, or a decline.

academic-08__base.text:
You asked for frankness, so here it is: **the data as you've described them favour H2, and your discussion currently argues against your own results.** I think your supervisor's "doesn't land" is about this.

**What the results show**

- The dominance correlation is near zero (r = .19, n.s.). With n = 64, the 95% CI runs roughly from −.06 to .42. That is not strong evidence for transfer, and it is not a clean null either, but it is the direct test of H1, and it did not come out in H1's favour.
- The input correlation is large (r = −.58, p < .001), and the sibling finding points the same way.
- Neuter clustering (61% of errors on the lowest-frequency class in child-directed input) is what a frequency account predicts.

**Where the discussion goes wrong**

1. **Paragraph 2 is not diagnostic.** Monolingual controls at 4% versus 23% in bilinguals shows that bilinguals err more. But bilingual children also receive less German input than monolinguals, so both H1 and H2 predict this gap. The comparison cannot support transfer over input.
2. **Paragraph 3 explains away the null.** "Our dominance measure may be too coarse" is a post hoc rescue. If the measure is standard, the reliability and validity should be reported. If you invoke measurement error, you need to show it, and the same logic would apply to your input estimates, which are parent-reported hours and probably noisier.
3. **Paragraph 4 understates the main result.** "Also played a role" describes a correlation of −.58 as a minor factor. It is the strongest effect in the study.
4. **Paragraph 5 treats the neuter finding as a side note.** It is possibly your most informative result. Frequency-based accounts predict exactly this concentration.
5. **Paragraph 6 reverses the evidence.** "Transfer remains the most plausible explanation, possibly modulated by input" cannot be defended given the data above. If anything, the defensible claim is the reverse.

**What I'd check before rewriting**

- **Partial correlations or a regression with both predictors.** Dominance and input are probably correlated. If dominance adds nothing once input is controlled, that is your key result, stated directly. If dominance predicts errors only among low-input children, that would be a more interesting pattern and could partly rescue a transfer account. Check this before you commit to a story.
- **Error substitution patterns.** When children err on neuter nouns, what do they produce instead? A systematic default (e.g., masculine *der* everywhere) would be a transfer-friendly signature, since it would suggest a reduced gender system. Diffuse substitution favours a frequency or retrieval account. This is the analysis that could still give transfer a fair hearing.
- **Whether the errors are lexical or systematic.** Are errors concentrated in a few items or spread across children?

**How far to restructure**

The discussion needs a substantial rewrite, but probably not a new study. The rewrite should:

- Lead with the input result and the neuter pattern.
- Report the dominance null plainly, with its CI, and state what it does and doesn't rule out. You can say transfer effects, if present, are small enough not to be detected here.
- Treat the monolingual comparison as showing that bilinguals err more, without attributing the gap to transfer.
- Discuss transfer as a hypothesis that was tested and not supported in this sample, and say what evidence would change that.

**The introduction**

Your literature review on transfer can stay, since it is still the relevant background. But if the introduction frames the thesis as "transfer explains gender errors in bilingual children," that framing is now contradicted by your own data, and the examiners will notice. You will likely need to reframe the research question so that the study's contribution is discriminating between transfer and input accounts. That is a stronger thesis than a confirmation, and the design (64 children, two competing predictions, one clear dissociation) supports it.

On the emotional side: a doctoral study that tests a hypothesis, finds it unsupported, and identifies the better-supported alternative is a respectable result. Reviewers and examiners generally respect a clear, honest reversal much more than a discussion that stretches the data to protect the original proposal.

If you share the analysis outputs (especially the partial correlation and the substitution data) or the current wording of your conclusion, I can help you draft the restructured discussion.

team-04__base.text:
Yes, I think the recommendation has a hidden dependency. The thing that feels off is probably this: **the processor dashboard is built on the same data that's broken.**

1. **The forecasts would be built on the paper-based data.** A volume forecast by collection centre is only as good as the weights behind it. At 40% of centres, those weights are handwritten, entered later, and wrong about 9% of the time. Processors would see the errors in the first month, and that's the kind of thing that ends a contract. You could also end up with a dashboard that's blind or unreliable exactly where volume is hardest to predict.

2. **The payment disputes are a supply-side risk, not just a morale issue.** Your marketplace depends on farmers staying loyal enough to keep delivering milk to the processors you're selling to. If 22k farmers are getting wrong payments and support tickets are up 60%, that churn directly undermines the volume the processors are paying for. I'd move "continued payment disputes" from a line item under Option A's risks to the main argument against it.

3. **The KES 14M is conditional pipeline, not contracted revenue.** "Will sign if they get a dashboard" is a real signal, but it's not ARR yet. Ask sales what probability they'd assign to each deal and whether any of the three have seen the data quality issue. A processor that discovers the 9% error rate during a pilot will walk away.

4. **The risks are framed asymmetrically.** Option B's main risk is losing deals, but those deals are conditional on a product that needs clean data. Losing them to a competitor is a real risk, but a competitor shipping a dashboard on bad data would have the same problem.

**Questions to answer before you send it:**
- What share of total milk volume comes through the paper-based centres? If the high-volume centres are the paper ones, the dashboard covers less than it appears to.
- Have the three processors specified what data quality they need, or whether they'd accept a dashboard that starts with digital centres only?
- Would they sign on a timeline that's 14 weeks out (B then A) rather than 8?
- What's the revenue at risk from farmer churn due to disputes? Even a rough number makes the comparison much more concrete.

**A different recommendation to consider:** Do B first, but scope it tightly: offline-first entry for the paper centres, with the goal of reducing errors and disputes. Then build A on the cleaned data, and use the 14 weeks to go back to the processors with a pilot covering the digital centres. You'd lose some time with the deals, but you'd avoid signing customers on a forecast you can't stand behind. With 11 months of runway, a roughly 14-week sequence leaves room to ship both.

If you do go with A, I'd at least make data quality a stated precondition, with a plan for the paper centres in the doc, so Wanjiru sees you've considered it.
